Athlete's foot is a type of fungal infection. If your baby has it, you may notice peeling skin between their toes. In more severe cases, the skin on their feet may crack and bleed. The skin can look red on white skin, but this may be less noticeable on brown or black skin. It can also be itchy for your little one, so you may notice them scratching their feet more than usual.
If you think your baby has athlete's foot, take them to your local pharmacist. They'll be able to prescribe a cream to clear up the infection.
Athlete's foot is a fungal infection that causes a red, itchy, moist rash, usually between the toes. It's rare in toddlers, but it may be more likely to happen if you take your child swimming a lot. This is because the fungus thrives in warm, damp areas like showers and changing rooms.
You can help to prevent athlete's foot by dressing your toddler in cotton socks, and drying between her toes properly after baths and swimming. Speak to your pharmacist before buying any over-the-counter treatments, as some aren't suitable for young children.

If your baby has acne, they may have it at birth, but it usually shows up after a couple of weeks. On white skin it looks like small, red spots (pimples), and whiteheads may also develop, sometimes surrounded by reddish skin. On brown and black skin the spots may be harder to see but the skin surrounding them may go darker. The spots are likely to appear on your baby's cheeks, but may also appear on their forehead and nose.
It’s normal for newborns to develop spots as their delicate skin adjusts to life in the outside world. Spots vary and may look like pimples, acne, or a rash. Usually, they’re harmless and soon go away. But occasionally a rash may mean your baby is unwell. Find out what’s causing your baby’s spots, whether you need to treat them, and when to call the doctor.
Why is my newborn’s face covered in pimples?
Your baby is likely to have a condition called milia, which is common in newborns and nothing to worry about. Your baby may have milia at birth or soon after. If your baby was born prematurely, milia may appear later than this.
You’ll see tiny raised spots, usually sprinkled across your baby’s nose, cheeks, forehead or around the eyes. The spots may look white or yellow, depending on your baby’s skin colour.
Milia happens when a protein called keratin gets trapped under your baby’s skin, forming tiny cysts. Keratin is found naturally in your baby’s skin and helps protect the outer layer.
Milia spots clear up on their own in a few weeks and won’t leave any blemishes.
What is erythema toxicum?
Erythema toxicum is a harmless blotchy, red or purple rash that affects about half of babies soon after birth, usually in the first couple of days.
The rash appears on the face, neck, upper arms, thighs, and central part of your baby’s body and doesn’t spread to the hands and feet. It will appear more red if your baby has white skin and more purple or deep burgundy if your baby has brown or black skin.
It’s not clear what causes erythema toxicum. One theory is that it happens as your baby’s immune system adjusts to the outside world.
In spite of the name, erythema toxicum is not toxic. It doesn’t mean your baby is ill, or has an allergy. It's unlikely to bother your baby, and it should clear up on its own in a few days to a week, though for a few babies the rash may come and go.
You don’t need to wash your baby’s skin more than usual, and don’t squeeze any of the spots. Just follow your baby’s usual gentle bathing and skincare routine. It won’t be long before your baby’s skin is back to normal.
Some parents like to smooth breastmilk on the spotty areas of their baby’s skin. It’s true that breastmilk can help to fight some baby infections, but there’s no proof it helps with erythema toxicum.
Occasionally, erythema toxicum in babies with dark brown or black skin may be confused with another harmless but rarer rash called transient neonatal pustular melanosis (TNPM).
TNPM affects babies with black or brown skin more than those with white skin. It’s not known what causes it. Unlike erythema toxicum, TNPM spots may spread to the hands and feet.
The spots aren’t sore for your baby, and are usually gone in a couple of weeks. The spots burst easily, though, leaving little flaky ring-shaped marks that may persist for a further few weeks.
Does my baby have acne?
It’s unlikely that your baby has true acne, which is more like the type of acne that may affect teenagers and adults.
True acne in babies is rare. It only affects about two in 100 babies, usually boys. The medical name for true acne in babies is infantile acne.
Baby acne more often describes the spots and rashes that are common in newborns as their skin adjusts to the outside world. For example, erythema toxicum is sometimes called baby acne.
Another common newborn rash is neonatal acne. Again, despite the name, neonatal acne isn’t really acne. Its medical name is neonatal cephalic pustulosis (NCP).
NCP may affect your baby from about three weeks. It’s harmless and affects nearly a quarter of newborns.
NCP causes fluid-filled pimples to appear on your baby’s face, and sometimes head and neck. It can look a bit like heat rash. It’s not known for sure what causes NCP. One theory is that it’s a reaction to a skin infection.
NCP won’t bother your baby but it’s understandable if it bothers you, as it can be quite noticeable. It shouldn’t need treating. Just wash your baby’s face with a gentle baby soap and water. You could ease off using any oily moisturisers on your baby’s face while the spots last. The spots should clear up without leaving any blemishes by the time your baby’s four months old.
How can I tell if my baby has infantile acne?
Infantile acne starts later than any other type of rash that may be called baby acne. It usually starts at around three or four months. It can cause more spots than other rashes and affects the face, mainly the cheeks. Infantile acne brings out red spots and bumps, often with whiteheads and blackheads. On dark brown and black skin, the red area around the spots can look purple or a deep burgundy colour.
Infantile acne usually clears up in a baby’s first year, but unlike other baby rashes, it can leave scars. This is especially the case for babies with severe outbreaks and babies with darker skin.
If you get treatment early on for your baby there’s less chance they will scar, so see your doctor as soon as you can if you’re worried your baby has infantile acne.
Your doctor will decide the best treatment, but it’s likely to include antiseptic or antibiotic cream for you to smooth on your baby’s skin.
If your baby has infantile acne that doesn’t go away after they reach a year old, be sure to go back to your doctor. Acne at this age that doesn’t clear up may be a sign that your child’s hormone balance needs checking.

Blepharitis is the name for swelling around the edges of your baby's eyelid. It's usually caused by a skin condition such as dermatitis, or a bacterial infection.
Blepharitis can make your baby's eyelashes appear crusty or greasy, and they may stick together. Your baby's eyelid may also burn or itch, and they may be upset and cry more than usual. However, blepharitis isn't normally serious, and it won't damage your baby's eye.
What is blepharitis?
Blepharitis happens when your baby's eyelids become red and sore. It usually affects both eyes.
As well as redness and swelling, you may also notice flakes or crusts around the bases of your baby's eyelashes. Blepharitis is likely to make your baby's eyes itchy, gritty and dry.
Blepharitis is caused by sensitivity to normally harmless skin bacteria and can be more likely to happen if your baby is prone to eczema. Blepharitis may also make your baby more likely to get a stye.
Your baby may rub their eyes more and be grouchier than normal, and may have trouble opening their eyes when they wake up.
Blepharitis is common, and although uncomfortable, it's usually harmless.
How should I treat my baby’s blepharitis?
If your baby has blepharitis, you'll be able to treat it at home. But if you're not sure whether it's blepharitis or something else, take them to your GP or your pharmacy to get them checked out first.
Blepharitis can keep coming back but it's possible to treat and keep at bay with a daily routine of warmth, massage and cleansing.
Here's how:
- Warmth: Soak cotton wool or a clean flannel in water that's hot but a safe temperature for your baby's delicate skin. Press gently onto your baby's closed eyelids for two or three minutes at a time.
- Massage: Straight afterwards, gently roll a clean finger over your baby's closed eyelids, in a downward motion towards the lashes on the upper eyelid, and upwards when moving along the lower eyelid. This can help the glands that line your baby's eyelids to release their moisturising fluid.
- Cleanse: Use a of piece of cotton wool, or a soft clean flannel, dipped in warm water to gently wipe along your baby's eyelash line. The aim is to remove any flakes.
Do this twice a day while your baby has blepharitis, and then once a day after it's cleared up to stop it coming back.
It can be hard to stick to this routine with a squirming baby. You can also ask your pharmacist for advice, as blepharitis is sometimes treated with eye wipes or pads.
If your baby’s eyes do not improve with regular cleaning, take them to your GP. Your GP may prescribe an antibiotic ointment if they suspect that the blepharitis has been caused by a bacterial infection.

If your baby's eyelid looks like there's a bump under it, they may have a chalazion. This is a painless bump or cyst that can appear under the upper or lower eyelid. The cyst is caused by a blocked gland in your baby's eyelid.
A chalazion is usually more annoying than painful for your baby. It should go away on its own after a month or so, though it can sometimes take longer. If your baby still has a chalazion after a month, see your doctor.
What is a chalazion?
A chalazion is a bump or cyst on the eyelid. It's usually painless, and should not bother your baby. It may look like a stye for the first couple of days.
Glands that run along your baby's eyelids produce an oily fluid that keeps your baby's eye moist. A chalazion happens when the oil blocks one of these glands.
The medical term for a chalazion is a meibomian cyst, because the glands that protect your baby's eyes are called meibomian glands.
Chalazions are more common on the upper eyelid than the lower. The cyst can start out as small as a poppy seed but may grow bigger. It's possible to have more than one chalazion at once, and in some cases, your baby's whole eyelid may appear swollen.
Your baby's chalazion should go away on its own, but this may take a few weeks or even months.
How should I treat my baby’s chalazion?
Chalazions do not usually need treating. Very rarely, they can become infected, so keep your baby's eyes clean. Twice a day, wipe your baby's eyes from the nose outward with a clean, moist piece of cotton wool.
You can also use a warm compress a couple of times a day, if your baby will tolerate it. Dip a clean flannel in warm water, squeeze it out, then place it over their eye for at least two minutes at a time. The warmth of the compress may help the cyst to soften and drain.
If your baby's chalazion is not getting better after a month, take them to see your GP. It may be that the cyst needs more time to fully clear up, but your doctor will be able to advise you. If you're not sure whether it's a chalazion or something else, see your GP sooner, particularly if your baby seems to be in any pain.

The first symptoms of chickenpox can include:
- fever
- aches and pains
- loss of appetite
A chickenpox rash starts as small spots that can appear anywhere on the body. They can be red, pink, darker or the same colour as surrounding skin. These then develop into tiny fluid-filled blisters, which are very itchy and may burst. They eventually scab over. There may be so many spots that they join up or there may be just a few.
What is chickenpox?
Chickenpox is a highly infectious illness caused by varicella-zoster virus, one of a group of herpes viruses. Most children will get chickenpox when they are young and it's usually a mild illness.
Once your child has caught the virus, symptoms can take between one week and three weeks to show.
What are the symptoms of chickenpox?
The most noticeable symptom is the rash. It starts as little spots which may appear red, pink, darker or the same colour as your baby's skin, depending on their skin tone. These spots may be harder to see on black or brown skin. The spots develop into tiny blisters within a few hours. You'll probably notice them first on your child's face. The spots will spread to their chest and tummy, and then to other parts of their body, appearing in crops.
There may be so many spots and blisters that they will appear to run into one another, or there may just be a few spots. The spots may bother your baby most in their mouth and throat, and around their genitals.
Your baby is likely to feel tired and ill, and may also have:
- fever
- aches and pains
- loss of appetite
How can I treat my baby's chickenpox?
You can treat your baby's chickenpox at home. It's a virus, so it can't be cured or prevented with antibiotics. Chickenpox goes away on its own after about a week.
Here's how to help your baby through a chickenpox infection:
- Give them plenty of fluids so they don't get dehydrated. Offer them extra breastfeeds or bottle feeds. If they are formula-fed, or eating solid foods, they can also have water.
- Bath your baby in cool or tepid water. Try putting bicarbonate of soda, or a sock full of oatmeal, in the water. There's no evidence that these home remedies ease itching, but many parents swear by them. Gently dab or pat your baby's skin dry after their bath.
- Soothe your baby's skin with a moisturiser or cooling gel. Ask your pharmacist about the best treatment. Moisturisers with extract of oatmeal may help to soothe irritated skin. Calamine lotion is traditionally recommended, but it can dry out your baby's skin, making it more itchy.
- Keep your baby's nails short, or put on cotton mitts, if they keep scratching themselves. This will help to prevent the spots from becoming infected and reduce the likelihood of scarring.
- Dress your baby in loose, cotton clothing to keep their skin cool and reduce itching.
You can also give your baby infant paracetamol if they have a temperature and to relieve their aches and pains. Your baby can have infant paracetamol from two months, as long as they were born after 37 weeks and weigh more than 4kg (9lb). Check the dosage information on the packet, or ask your doctor or pharmacist.
Doctors are more cautious about recommending infant ibuprofen, as it may increase the risk of your baby either developing an infection in their spots, or of making an existing infection worse. Infections like this are uncommon, but they can lead to serious illness.
If your baby is over one year old and the itching is particularly troublesome at night, you could ask your health visitor or pharmacist about giving them the antihistamine chlorphenamine (Piriton). As well as easing your baby's itching, it has a sedative effect which may help them to sleep more easily.
When should I take my baby to the doctor?
If your baby is less than four weeks old, take them to the doctor if they've been exposed to chickenpox, whether or not they're showing symptoms. Chickenpox can be more dangerous for very young babies.
Your doctor may refer your baby to hospital for treatment by a paediatrician. There are two types of treatment for young babies who've been exposed to chickenpox:
- Babies who are not showing any chickenpox symptoms can be protected against the illness with varicella-zoster immunoglobulin (VZIG). VZIG contains antibodies against the chickenpox virus.
- Babies who are showing symptoms of chickenpox are treated with aciclovir, which can lessen the severity of the symptoms.
If your baby has painful spots in his mouth, they may be so reluctant to drink that they become dehydrated. Signs of dehydration are fewer wet nappies than usual, dark yellow wee, and tearless crying. If you see these signs, take your baby to the doctor.
Sometimes, chickenpox spots can become infected with bacteria. A bacterial infection will make the skin around your baby's spots look red and swollen, and their skin will be tender to the touch. Take your baby to the doctor if you see these signs. Your doctor can give you antibiotic cream or medicine for your baby to clear the infection from the spots.
If you're worried about your baby, or they don't seem to be getting better, take them to the doctor. Chickenpox usually gets better, not worse, so you need to get advice if your baby doesn't seem to be fighting it off.
Very rarely, chickenpox can lead to more serious conditions, such as pneumonia or swelling of the brain (encephalitis).
Dial 999 and ask for an ambulance, or take your baby to your hospital's accident and emergency (A&E) department if they:
- have difficulty breathing
- have a seizure
- become unusually drowsy, faint and floppy
Chickenpox is a notifiable disease in Northern Ireland or Scotland. If you live in either of these places it's helpful if you tell your doctor about your baby's illness, even if you don't make a doctor's appointment.
Should I keep my baby at home while they've got chickenpox?
Your baby is contagious until their spots have crusted over, which usually takes around five days. Until then, you'll have to keep them away from nursery, or places where they may have close contact with other people. This includes children's centres, soft play areas, and parent and baby groups.
Some nurseries and childminders have their own policies about how long children with chickenpox should stay at home, so check with your childcare provider if you're not sure.
Keeping your baby comfortable at home will also help to protect other people from catching chickenpox, because it spreads so easily.
It's possible to catch chickenpox from being in the same room as someone with the virus for 15 minutes. Very young babies and non-immune adults, especially pregnant women, can become seriously ill from chickenpox.
This doesn't mean that you have to be house-bound for the whole time your baby's ill. If he's well enough, you can try some outdoor activities that don't require close contact with others. Going to the park, feeding the ducks, or popping to the shops at quiet times will help you both get some fresh air and ward off cabin fever.
Can I catch chickenpox from my baby?
If you've never had chickenpox before, you could catch it from your baby. See your doctor if you think you have chickenpox, as it's usually a more severe illness for adults. This is especially important if you're pregnant, or think you may be pregnant. Chickenpox can be very harmful to an unborn baby.
If you've had chickenpox before, there's only a very remote chance that you'll get it again. The varicella-zoster virus stays in your body, though, and may be triggered as shingles if you ever become run-down through stress and illness.
Is there a chickenpox vaccine?
Yes, but it's not part of the routine childhood vaccination programme offered by the NHS. You can pay for your baby to have it privately through larger branches of some chemists.
Immunisation against chickenpox uses a live vaccine, with just enough of the weakened virus to cause antibodies to form in your baby's body.
There's a small chance that a baby or child could develop a mild infection following the vaccination and pass it on to a non-immune or vulnerable person they see a lot, such as a family member or carer. It's useful to be aware of this if you're planning to have your baby vaccinated.
Once your baby has been vaccinated, he's likely to be protected against chickenpox for between 10 years and 20 years.

disease_information:
What is shingles?
Shingles (herpes zoster) is an infection caused by the varicella-zoster virus, the same virus that causes chickenpox. After recovering from chickenpox, the virus can remain inactive in the body and reactivate years later as shingles. Although it is rare in babies, it can occur if a baby was exposed to chickenpox during pregnancy or as a newborn.

What are the symptoms of shingles?
The first signs of shingles often include a burning, tingling, or painful sensation on the skin, usually limited to one side of the body. Within a few days, a red rash appears in the same area, followed by fluid-filled blisters. These blisters eventually scab over. Shingles can also cause fever, headache, tiredness, and sensitivity to light. In infants, the rash may be difficult to distinguish from other skin conditions but is usually accompanied by discomfort or irritability.

How can I treat my baby's shingles?
If your baby has shingles, treatment focuses on relieving symptoms and preventing complications:
- Keep the rash clean and dry to reduce the risk of infection.
- Dress your baby in loose, soft cotton clothing.
- Use cool compresses or oatmeal baths to ease itching.
- Apply pediatrician-recommended creams or lotions.
- Infant paracetamol can be used to reduce fever and discomfort (follow dosage instructions).
- Avoid using ibuprofen unless advised by a doctor.
Antiviral medication may be prescribed by a doctor in some cases to lessen the severity or duration of the illness, especially in very young or immunocompromised babies.

When should I take my baby to the doctor?
See a doctor if:
- Your baby is under 1 month old and has symptoms of shingles.
- The rash is near the eyes or causes swelling around the face.
- Your baby has a high fever, is unusually drowsy, or seems very unwell.
- The blisters appear to be infected (red, swollen, or filled with pus).
- You are unsure whether it is shingles or another skin condition.
Prompt medical attention can prevent complications such as bacterial infections or, in rare cases, nerve pain.

Should I keep my baby at home while they have shingles?
Yes. Your baby is contagious if the rash is in the blister phase and not yet scabbed over. Until the blisters have dried and crusted, avoid contact with:
- Pregnant individuals who have not had chickenpox or the vaccine.
- People with weakened immune systems.
- Newborn babies.
Your baby should stay home from daycare or group activities until the rash has completely crusted over, which usually takes about 7–10 days. This will help prevent the spread of the virus to others.

The first time your baby catches the cold sore virus, it will probably give them swollen gums and a sore mouth, which will make them drool. Your baby may also have a fever and swollen glands in their neck, and seem generally under the weather. Soon afterwards, you may notice painful blisters inside their mouth, which develop into ulcers. These can last for up to three weeks.
The next time your baby gets a cold sore, the symptoms are likely to be much milder. Your baby will probably develop one or more blisters on or near their lips, which should clear up within a couple of weeks. Cold sores are contagious so avoid kissing your baby on the lips.
Cold sores are caused by the herpes simplex virus. They're very common, and most people carry the virus in their bodies. If you get a cold sore, you need to avoid passing it on to your baby. This is because herpes simplex can pose a risk to vulnerable babies and in very rare cases, can cause a serious disease called neonatal herpes. Find out how to protect your baby from the virus, and what to do if they get a cold sore.
What is a cold sore?
Cold sores are small, red blisters that can crop up in your baby's mouth, or on or near their lips. They are caused by the herpes simplex virus. Despite their name, cold sores have nothing to do with colds and they affect people all year round.
The herpes simplex virus is very common. Up to seven out of 10 people carry it. Some people with the virus never have any cold sores, so may not know they have it.
A cold sore usually starts with a tingling feeling, followed a day or so later by the appearance of a blister or cluster of blisters. The blisters are fluid-filled and packed with the virus. Over several days, the painful blisters burst and ooze before scabbing over.
Cold sores are infectious from the tingle until they're fully healed. The whole outbreak usually lasts for between seven and 10 days.
There's no cure for cold sores. Once it's inside the body, the herpes simplex virus hides from the immune system. However, you can treat cold sore symptoms with over-the-counter medicines.
Are cold sores harmful for babies?
It depends on your baby's age. Cold sores are harmful for newborns because their immune systems are still developing.
Very rarely, herpes simplex can cause a serious illness called neonatal herpes in newborns who are less than four weeks old. Only 10 in 100,000 births across the world are affected by neonatal herpes.
Most babies with neonatal herpes catch it during vaginal birth because their mum has a new outbreak of genital herpes. It's much less likely for a newborn to get neonatal herpes from someone with a cold sore, perhaps through a kiss. But it's still important for you and anyone else with a cold sore to make sure it doesn’t come into contact with your baby because neonatal herpes can be life threatening.
Thankfully it's also very rare for newborns to get cold sores from someone else. Most young babies have natural protection from their mum's antibodies, picked up during their time in the womb. This protection usually lasts for the first six months after birth.
However, if you got your first-ever cold sore, called a primary infection, in the last three months of pregnancy, your newborn won't be protected. Herpes simplex antibodies made by your body won't have had time to cross the placenta before your baby's born.
How do cold sores spread?
Cold sores spread easily, usually through kisses. During a cold sore outbreak the virus may also be in the saliva, so dropping a kiss from the other side of the mouth will not protect your baby.
If your baby does get herpes simplex they may develop a cold sore soon after being infected. The virus stays in their body for the rest of their life, lying dormant in nerve cells. The virus can then wake up and trigger cold sores. Triggers for cold sores may include:
- feeling run-down, tired or stressed.
- coughs, colds and flu especially with a fever
- being in strong sunlight.
- sudden changes in temperature, for example, going into a hot room after being out in freezing weather.
What are the symptoms of a cold sore?
Your baby's first cold sore outbreak is most likely to be inside their mouth and on their gums, rather than on the lips. A cold sore infection inside your baby's mouth is called gingivostomatitis. At the start of the infection you may notice your baby:
- Has a fever.
- Seems to have a sore throat, with swollen glands in their neck.
- Is grizzly and lethargic.
- Has a sore mouth and is drooling. The soreness may put your baby off eating and drinking.
Soon after you'll see crops of painful blisters inside your baby's mouth, on the tongue, gums, roof and floor of the mouth. The blisters develop into ulcers that may have yellowish-grey centres.
A flare-up of gingivostomatitis is likely to last for about two or three weeks. Your baby will be sore and miserable while it lasts, but gingivostomatitis is likely only to happen once.
The next time your baby has an outbreak they're more likely to have a cold sore or sores on the lips, and nothing inside the mouth.
Do I need to take my baby to the doctor for a cold sore?
Take your baby to the doctor if they're younger than six months, or if you're worried about them, whatever their age.
For older babies and children, cold sores, though uncomfortable, are usually harmless. They should clear up on their own without the need for a trip to the doctor. Your pharmacist can advise you on the best way to treat your child's cold sore.
However, if your baby has gingivostomatitis it may put them off drinking, making them dehydrated.
Encourage your baby to have small drinks as often as possible. If you're worried your baby is dehydrated, see your doctor. Signs of dehydration include:
- drowsiness
- fast breathing
- tearless crying
- dark yellow, strong-smelling wee
- a dry nappy for the past 12 hours
- cold and blotchy-looking hands and feet
If your baby becomes seriously dehydrated during the gingivostomatitis outbreak, your doctor may admit them to hospital for a short while. Hospital staff will nurse your baby through the worst of the illness, giving fluids via a drip and pain relief if necessary.
If you're not sure whether your baby's blisters and ulcers are cold sores, see your doctor. It's possible that the sores may be something else, such as impetigo.
How can I treat my baby's gingivostomatitis or cold sore?
Antiviral creams and other over-the-counter remedies can treat an outbreak, but whether they're suitable depends on the type of infection:
Gingivostomatitis
If your baby has gingivostomatitis, your doctor won't recommend antiviral cream for you to apply. It's distressing for babies to have it put in their mouths and it washes off too easily.
Instead, the best way to care for your baby is to:
- Offer plenty of their usual milk. If your baby is formula-fed, they can have cooled, boiled water too.
- Give easy-to-eat soft foods such as yoghurt or soup, if your baby's old enough. Cold or cool foods may be easier for your baby to manage.
- Give the correct dose of infant paracetamol or infant ibuprofen to ease pain.
If your baby is a thumb-sucker, the virus may transfer to his thumb or fingers. This can cause a painful blister called a herpetic whitlow.
Cold sores
You can ease your baby's discomfort by following these steps:
- Use an over-the-counter antiviral cream as soon as the cold sore appears. Ask your pharmacist which type is suitable for your baby, as some cold sore creams are not recommended for children under 12 years. An antiviral cream may speed up healing, if used early enough. Always wash your hands after treating your baby.
- Keep your baby's sore from cracking and bleeding by gently smoothing on unscented lip balm. Petroleum jelly also works fine.
- If your baby is old enough you can give them an ice pop to suck on to ease the pain and get some fluids.
- If your baby's mouth is sore and they don't want to drink, try different ways to encourage them. Offer short, frequent breastfeeds or bottle feeds. You could also try using a syringe gently inserted in the side of their mouth to give them extra water.
- To ease your baby's pain and any fever, you can give them the correct dose of infant paracetamol or infant ibuprofen.
Rarely, the virus can spread to other parts of the body through touch. This is very unlikely to happen to your baby, but it may help to be aware of how it happens just in case.
A rare complication is eye disease, when someone touches a cold sore, then touches their eyes. It's natural for babies and young children to rub their eyes, especially when they're tired or grizzly. You could try anti-scratch mittens while the cold sore is at the oozing stage.
If your baby does develop sore eyes or blisters around their eyes, see your GP as soon as possible. Your baby may need antiviral drugs to protect their eyes from being damaged by the infection.
Anti-scratch mittens are also useful if your baby has eczema. Very rarely, herpes simplex can infect eczema patches causing the severe infection, eczema herpeticum.
You don't need to keep your baby away from nursery or preschool if they have gingivostomatitis or a cold sore, provided they are otherwise well.
Can I breastfeed my baby if they have a cold sore?
You can breastfeed your baby, if you like, but it may be best to speak to your health visitor or practice nurse first. The difficulty is that by the time you notice your baby has sores, the virus will probably have had contact with your breasts. It is possible to get a herpes simplex infection on your nipples or breasts, but it is very rare.
An infection on your nipples or breasts can be very painful and give you a fever. If you do develop sores, see your doctor. They may recommend an antiviral treatment.
You'll need to stop putting your baby to your infected breast until after the sores have healed. If only one of your breasts is affected, you can still feed from your other breast.
In the meantime you can express milk from your infected breast to keep up your supply. Your baby can have the expressed milk, as long as you're sure it's had no contact with the sores. However if there's any chance of contact, throw it away in case the virus has infected the milk.
Wash your hands after touching your breasts, and clean and sterilise your pump attachments after you've expressed.
How can I prevent my baby getting a cold sore?
The best way to protect your baby from cold sores is to stop anyone who has an active sore from kissing them or touching their skin. This is especially important if your baby is newborn.
It can be hard not to kiss your newborn when it's such an instinctive thing to do, but it is safest to wait until the sore has gone. You can buy patches for cold sores, but these are to hide the sore and relieve pain. They aren't designed to stop the virus from spreading, so don't rely on them to protect your baby from kisses.
You can still show your baby how much you love them by cuddling them, ideally skin-to-skin, and chatting and singing to them.
Keep your baby's flannels and towels separate from the rest of the family's to prevent cross-contamination.
You can also protect your baby in lots of practical ways. If you get a cold sore, wash your hands after touching it or putting treatment on your sore. Also wash your hands before breastfeeding your baby.
Once your baby has the herpes simplex virus, you can prevent further outbreaks by keeping them out of direct sunlight. Exposure to sunlight can trigger an outbreak.
If you go outside on a sunny day, cover your baby with a sunscreen of at least SPF 15. Also apply a lip balm that contains sunscreen.

A pink watery eye may be a sign of conjunctivitis. You may also notice a discharge that makes your baby’s eyelashes stick together. Conjunctivitis can be caused by an allergy or an infection.
Infective conjunctivitis is caused by a bacterial or viral infection and it is very contagious. It often starts in one eye, but can easily spread to the other one, too. If your child is otherwise well they should be able to go to childcare or nursery as normal.
The white of my baby's eye is pink. Could he have conjunctivitis?
If your baby's eyes look pink, red or bloodshot, he may have conjunctivitis. The name comes from "conjunctiva", which is the name for the membrane that lines your baby's eyelids and covers the white part of his eye. Conjunctivitis happens when this membrane becomes inflamed. It can be itchy and uncomfortable for your baby, but it's usually completely harmless.
What causes conjunctivitis?
Conjunctivitis can be caused by:
- a viral or bacterial infection
- allergies such as hayfever or pet allergies
- irritation from something getting in your baby’s eye
Viral and bacterial conjunctivitis are highly contagious, and can easily be passed from person to person.
What are the symptoms of conjunctivitis?
The most noticeable symptom is the whites of your baby's eyes turning pink, red or bloodshot. His eyes may also be much more watery than usual, or you may notice a thicker discharge coming from them. This can make his eyelids crusty, which may make it more difficult for him to open his eyes after sleeping.
Conjunctivitis usually affects both eyes, sometimes starting in one eye then spreading to the other. It can be itchy or uncomfortable for your baby, so you'll probably find that he's restless and grumpy, and he may keep rubbing his eyes.
It can be difficult to tell which type of conjunctivitis your baby has, but his symptoms may give you a clue:
- Viral infections can make your baby's eyes gritty and uncomfortable, so if he seems to be in pain, this is the most likely cause.
- Thick yellow, white or green discharge is a sign that your baby’s conjunctivitis is more likely to be caused by a bacterial infection.
- If your baby's eyes become red, watery and itchy after contact with an allergen (such as pets, dust, or when the pollen count is high), he may have an allergy.
- If you notice that your baby has something in his eye, it's more likely to be down to irritation. This can also happen if his eyes react to something in his environment, such as cigarette smoke or chlorine in a swimming pool.
What should I do if I think my baby has conjunctivitis?
If your baby is under a month old, see your GP as soon as possible. Red or pink eyes in a newborn can sometimes If your baby is over a month old, and his eye is just a bit pink, there’s normally no need to worry. Follow the hygiene tips in the section below for two weeks to see if it helps clear up your baby’s conjunctivitis.
How should I care for my baby while he has conjunctivitis?
If your baby's eyelashes are sticky and crusty, you can gently clean them to make him more comfortable. Boil some water and allow it to cool completely. Soak a piece of cotton wool and gently rub his closed eyelid and eyelashes from the centre outwards. Use a fresh piece of cotton wool for the other eye.
If your baby’s eyes seem to be bothering him, you can also soak a flannel in cool, boiled water, and hold it over his eyes for a few minutes to give him some relief.
If your baby’s conjunctivitis has not improved after two weeks, see your GP. She’ll take a close look at your baby's eyes and ask you questions about his symptoms. She'll offer you different treatments depending on what she thinks is causing your baby's conjunctivitis:
- Bacterial infection: bacterial conjunctivitis often gets better on its own within a week. If your baby has a particularly bad case, or isn’t getting better, your GP may prescribe antibiotic cream or eye drops to clear up the infection. Make sure your baby takes the whole course, even if his eyes start to look better.
- Viral infection: a viral infection should clear up on its own within a few days to two weeks. If your baby's eyes are bothering him, your pharmacist can recommend ointment to help him feel better while he recovers.
- Allergies: if your little one's eyes are reacting to something in his environment, the best way to help him feel better is to avoid the thing he's allergic to. If this isn't possible, your GP may prescribe medicine such as antihistamines to help him feel better. Learn more about allergies in babies.
- Irritation: conjunctivitis due to irritation usually goes away on its own. If there's something stuck in your baby's eye, your GP may flush it out with water, or gently remove it with a damp cotton bud.
How can I stop my baby’s conjunctivitis from spreading?
Conjunctivitis that's caused by a viral or bacterial infection is very contagious. The following tips will help to prevent it spreading to the rest of your family:
- When you notice your baby rubbing his eyes, gently move his hands away.
- Wash your baby's hands regularly, especially when you notice him touching his eyes.
- Keep your baby's towels, bedding and face cloths separate, and wash them frequently on a hot wash.
If your child is otherwise well, he should be able to go to childcare or preschool as normal. However, every nursery and childminder has their own policy, so it’s a good idea to give them a ring first, just in case they'd rather he stays at home for a few days.

Cradle cap is common in newborns and can look like a bad case of dandruff. On white skin it can show up as large areas of white or yellow scaly patches. On black or brown skin, the affected area can look pink with white or grey scales.
Over time, the scales can become flaky so they rub off easily, just like dandruff, but often with bits of your baby's hair attached.
Cradle cap can cover the whole of your baby's scalp. It can also appear on your baby's face, and other places like their nappy area.
What is cradle cap?
Cradle cap (seborrhoeic dermatitis) is a common and harmless skin condition that often affects young babies. It usually appears on the scalp or face, and looks like a bad case of dandruff. It will normally go away on its own within a few months, without any treatment
Your baby is most likely to develop cradle cap in the first few months after the birth. If so, you'll notice greasy, yellow or brown scales appearing on her scalp. On white skin, the area may also look a bit red. On black or brown skin, cradle cap may look lighter or darker than the surrounding skin.
Over time, the scales can start to become flaky so they rub off easily, often with bits of your baby's hair attached. But don't worry, the hair will grow back!
Less commonly, seborrhoeic dermatitis can also affect other areas, such as your baby's face, neck, nappy area, armpits, or the backs of her knees.
Although the condition can look unsightly, it's not usually itchy and won't cause your baby any discomfort.
Your baby's cradle cap will probably clear up within a few weeks or months. Most children are free of cradle cap by the time they're six months old.
How did my baby get cradle cap?
Experts aren't sure exactly what causes cradle cap. It's thought that it may be more likely if your baby has particularly oily skin. There's also some evidence that a type of yeast called malassezia may play a part. However, we need more research to be sure.
One thing is certain, though: cradle cap is not caused by poor hygiene, so there's no need to worry that you're not bathing your baby often enough.
It's also not contagious, so touching or stroking your baby's head won't pass it on.
How can I get rid of my baby's cradle cap?
Your baby's cradle cap should disappear on its own within a few weeks or months. In the meantime, you can try the following techniques to gently remove the scales:
- Regularly wash your baby's hair with baby shampoo, then loosen the flakes using a soft brush. You can buy brushes specially designed for cradle cap online or at your local pharmacy, but any soft brush will do the job, including a new toothbrush with soft bristles.
- If simply shampooing and brushing doesn't work, you can try softening the scales first. Rub a mild baby oil, vegetable oil (such as coconut oil) or almond oil into your baby's scalp before putting her down for the night, then try shampooing and brushing again in the morning. Avoid using sunflower oil or olive oil on your baby's scalp, as these aren't good for her skin.
- The tips above should help to remove the worst of the flakes and make your baby's scalp look better. If not, speak to your pharmacist. She can recommend an emollient cream or a special cradle cap shampoo, and explain how to use it safely.
If your baby has eczema, avoid using shampoo. Instead, use coconut oil or her usual emollient cream to soften the cradle cap. You can then clean off the scales by washing her scalp with emollient and water.
It can be tempting to pick at the scaly patches on your baby's head, but try not to. Picking at it can leave sore patches that could become infected.
See your GP if your baby's cradle cap:
- seems to be itchy and uncomfortable for your baby
- looks red and swollen, or starts bleeding
- spreads to other areas of her face or body
In these cases, your GP may prescribe an antifungal cream to help clear it up.
In most cases, however, cradle cap is an annoying but harmless condition that should go away on its own.

Pus coming out of your baby's ear is a sure sign of an ear infection. Your baby will probably also have a fever and be generally unwell.
Ear infections are common in babies. Signs of an ear infection are your baby tugging or rubbing their ear, and reacting less to sounds because their ear is blocked. Ear infections can also cause earache, which is likely to make your baby grouchy and unsettled. The infection should clear up by itself after a few days, and will not normally need medical treatment. Most young children have at least two ear infections before they are five years old. Find out how to care for your baby while they have an ear infection.
How can I tell if my baby has an ear infection?
It can be difficult to tell if your baby is younger than six months. If your baby has a cough or runny nose with a fever, they could have an ear infection too.
Other signs you may notice are your baby:
- rubbing or pulling their ear a lot
- not reacting to sounds as much as usual
- getting hot and grumpy, and going off feeding
- losing their balance, if they are walking
If your baby has an earache, it does not necessarily mean they have an ear infection. Earache can be caused by other things, such as a build-up of uninfected mucus in the ear from a cold. Teething pain can sometimes be felt as pain in the ear, too.
If you're not sure what's causing your baby's earache, ask your pharmacist for advice.
How common are ear infections?
Ear infections are very common in babies and young children, especially during winter.
Your baby is most likely to get an ear infection between the ages of six months and two years. Most children have had at least two or more ear infections by the time they start school.
What has caused my baby’s ear infection?
Ear infections are usually caused by viruses and bacteria.
There are two main types of ear infection:
- middle ear infections (otitis media)
- outer ear infections (otitis externa), also known as swimmer's ear
This article is about middle ear infections. You can read more about outer ear infections in our article on swimmer's ear in babies.
Your baby's middle ear contains the eardrum. There is a small air-filled space behind the eardrum. This space is connected to the back of your baby's throat by a tiny channel called the Eustachian tube.
When your baby has a cold, mucus can fill the Eustachian tube and get into the space behind the eardrum. This mucus can become infected by viruses or bacteria or both, causing a middle ear infection.
How can my baby’s ear infection be treated?
Just like colds, ear infections usually clear up on their own, but it's a good idea to take your baby to your GP if:
- your baby is younger than three months old
- symptoms do not get better after three days
- your baby seems to be in a lot of pain
- there is swelling around your baby's ear, or pus coming out of it
- your baby has a very high temperature
- your baby has other health conditions
- both of your baby’s ears are affected
Your GP will look inside your baby's ear. They may just recommend painkillers such as paracetamol if there seems to be a viral infection which will get better by itself. They will only prescribe antibiotics if your baby appears to have a bacterial infection which is not settling.
You can give your baby infant paracetamol or infant ibuprofen to ease pain and reduce any fever. Check the packaging for the correct dose and age range for your baby. If you're not sure, ask your pharmacist for guidance.
Keeping up your baby's fluids will help them to recover. Offer plenty of breastfeeds. If your baby is formula-fed or on solids, offer extra water rather than more milk.
If your baby’s ear infection is not getting better, with or without treatment, take them back to your GP. If left untreated, ear infections can sometimes lead to hearing loss or, rarely, an infection that spreads more widely.
What can I do to prevent my baby getting an ear infection?
Ear infections are hard to prevent, because they are often caused by common cold viruses.
However, babies may be less likely to get an ear infection if they:
- are breastfed, as breastmilk protects babies against infections
- grow up in a smoke-free home
- are supported to sit up, rather than lying flat, for milk feeds
- have had the pneumococcal vaccine
Not giving your baby a dummy after they're six months old can also help to prevent ear infections. Babies who have persistent reflux, or gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD), are more likely to get ear infections more often. Managing GORD with the help of your doctor can protect your baby against getting lots of ear infections.

If your baby has eczema, they may have dry, itchy and cracked areas of skin. On white skin eczema can look red. On brown and black skin eczema is ashen brown, purple or grey. It can appear anywhere on the body, but it's most likely to crop up on your baby’s face and hands, and in skin creases, such as around your baby's elbows and knees.
There may be times when your baby doesn't have any symptoms at all, and other times when their symptoms are more noticeable (flare-ups).
Baby eczema: causes, symptoms, treatments and creams
Eczema is a dry, itchy skin condition that affects many babies in their first year. Eczema can be difficult to manage. It can make your baby grizzly and affect how well they sleep, and it can keep coming back. Unfortunately, eczema can't be prevented completely, but there's plenty you can do to ease it and reduce outbreaks. Read on to find out what causes eczema, how to soothe your baby's skin, and when to get medical help.
What does eczema look like?
If your baby has eczema they'll have patches of dry, scaly, irritated skin. Babies most often get eczema on their faces, scalps, outside of their elbows and on the front of their knees. If you notice your baby scratching at any of the dry patches they can reach, it could be eczema. Eczema is always itchy.
Eczema is often described as a pink or red rash but it how it looks depends on your baby's skin colour. It'll look pink or red if your baby's skin is white or light brown. On dark brown and black skin, the redness is harder to see. Eczema is more likely to appear purple, grey or ashy.
If your baby has been scratching a lot, it may make the patches of eczema appear slightly raised. This can help to diagnose it, whatever your baby's skin tone
There's no cure for eczema, but it can be soothed with treatments and many babies grow out of it eventually.
If you're worried about eczema ask your health visitor, practice nurse, or GP to examine your baby. Babies are prone to rashes and it's best to have a health professional diagnose eczema.
Why has my baby got eczema?
We don't know exactly what causes eczema, but it's usually a mixture of things. Eczema and other allergies, such as asthma and hay fever, tend to run in families. The medical name for eczema is atopic dermatitis. Atopic means a tendency to have allergies.
Your baby is more prone to eczema if their skin is often dry, and this tendency can be inherited too. People with eczema usually have less of a natural oily barrier in their skin. This means it's easier for skin to dry out and for substances to get in and cause itching. Your baby's skin will need plenty of extra moisturising to make up for this.
Eczema can get worse if your baby's skin is irritated, or triggered, by a substance or illness. These outbreaks of inflammation are known as flares, or flare-ups. A substance that causes a flare-up is called an allergen. Allergens are usually harmless, but people with eczema have a reaction because their immune system reads them as potentially harmful.
Your baby's eczema may come and go. Eczema is a complex condition, and it can be upsetting and frustrating when you can't work out why it's happening to your baby.
What can trigger my baby's eczema flare-ups?
Common triggers and allergens for eczema in babies and children include:
- Soaps, bath and skincare products, and laundry detergents.
- Synthetic or woollen fabrics. Some cotton dyes can cause sensitivity too.
- Allergens in the home or outside. These may include pet fur, pollen, and dust.
- Foods, such as cow's milk, egg, wheat, soya and peanuts.
- Extreme changes in temperature, whether hot or cold.
- Skin infections caused by some bacteria and viruses.
- Tiredness, teething, or having a cold can leave your baby more vulnerable to a flare-up.
Can I do anything to prevent my baby's eczema flare-ups?
You can't prevent your baby having eczema in the first place, but there's plenty you can do to make your baby comfortable and guard against flare-ups.
Most important is to moisturise your baby's skin with an emollient. Applying an emollient helps to keep water locked into your baby's skin. Water plumps up your baby's skin cells, helping them to form a stronger barrier with fewer gaps to let irritants through.
Emollients come as lotions, creams, and ointments, and as bath and shower products. Use a moisturiser that’s as greasy as possible. You may need to try a few different products before you find the one that suits your baby's skin best. Don't use aqueous cream, as this can irritate your baby's skin and may make their eczema worse.
Bathing your baby with an emollient bath or shower product, called a soap substitute, will also help. Take care, though, as emollient cleansers can make your baby slippery to bathe.
Do keep using emollients, even when your baby's skin is clear. This is especially important if allergies run in your family. Not only do emollients work well to ease your baby's eczema, there's also a chance they may protect your baby in the longer term.
Doctors are looking into whether using emollients in the first few months gives babies longer term protection against eczema and other allergies. The idea is that keeping out allergens early on helps to stop babies from becoming sensitised to them.
Emollients are excellent moisturisers, but they are oily. Fabrics and clothes that have soaked-in emollients can catch fire more easily. Always be even more careful than usual with your baby around candles and open fires.
Here is the best way to use emollients on your baby's skin:
- Use an emollient from a pump-action dispenser or with a spatula in a tub to keep the product free from germs.
- Dab the emollient on your baby's skin. Then smooth it on using gentle, downward strokes, following the line of your baby's hair growth. There's no need to rub it in.
- Apply the emollient several times a day if necessary.
- Bathe your baby daily with a soap substitute. Afterwards, gently pat your baby's skin with a clean towel and re-apply emollient while their skin is still damp. This will lock in even more moisture.
here are other ways you can reduce your baby's chances of having a flare-up:
- Keep your baby's fingernails trimmed, to reduce soreness from scratching. You could also buy them anti-scratch mittens.
- Dress your baby in soft, comfortable cotton clothes and don't put wool next to their skin.
- If your baby has started solids, their hands and cheeks may flare up with food and drink smears. It may help to protect these areas with an emollient before your baby has a snack or a meal.
- Double rinse your baby's clothes, bedding, and towels to remove laundry detergent residue. Some parents swear by non-bio for their baby's washing, but there's no proof that the enzymes in biological products trigger eczema. They key is to choose an unfragranced product and use the minimum amount necessary to get a good clean.
- Keep the space where your baby sleeps cool, around 18 degrees C, as getting too hot and sweaty can cause a flare-up.
- If you take your baby swimming, smooth on emollient beforehand. Afterwards, rinse your baby well with fresh water to remove chlorine, and moisturise again thoroughly.
Pet and house dust mite allergies tend to affect children more than babies. It's normal to put off chores like vacuuming when you're busy with a baby. So try not to stress about keeping your home dust-free, as it's unlikely to affect your baby's eczema.
Could my baby's eczema be caused by a food allergy?
If your baby has been diagnosed with eczema, they may be more likely to have a food allergy.
If you're exclusively breastfeeding, it’s unlikely that anything you've eaten will trigger your baby's eczema. Although in some babies , taking in cow’s milk through your breastmilk can cause cow's milk allergy (CMA) which can make existing eczema worse. Talk to your GP if you’re worried your baby has CMA.
If you're formula feeding and think your baby may have CMA, speak to a health professional before trying different formulas. They will be able to help you find the best milk for your baby.
Trying out first foods is bound to be a worry if your baby has eczema. Speak to your health visitor, practice nurse or GP for advice when it comes to weaning. They may advise you to introduce new foods in small amounts, and keep a food diary to note down any reactions your baby may have.
Don't cut anything out of your baby's diet without getting medical advice. Your baby is growing fast and needs a range of foods to stay healthy.
Your GP may refer your baby to a hospital allergy team if they think you and your baby need more specialist support or they may suggest a special diet to try.

What if my baby's eczema gets worse?
For some babies, emollient alone is not enough to ease eczema. If your baby has moderate or severe eczema, keep an using emollient, but see your GP. They may recommend more treatments:
Steroid cream or ointment
Your baby may need a short spell of treatment with a mild steroid cream or ointment to smooth onto the affected areas of their skin.
Steroids are medicines that reduce redness, swelling and itchiness and speed up healing. They work by supporting the body's natural hormones and slightly damping down the immune system's reaction to harmless irritants.
Steroids come in different strengths. The mildest cream should be enough to give your baby relief from soreness and itchiness. It's only in cases where a baby's eczema is severe that a step up to moderate-strength cream is needed, and only for a short time. The strongest creams are not recommended for babies.
Steroids are very safe and work well to ease symptoms and protect delicate skin from damage. Some people worry about steroids because they can cause side-effects, such as thinning of the skin. But this only happens if steroids are used at the wrong strength, or for too long, or are not applied properly.
Your GP will be careful to prescribe the right course of treatment for your baby. They will answer any questions you have and will explain how to apply the cream, how much to use and for how long.
Bandages and wraps
If your baby has severe eczema that's making them very unsettled, your GP may suggest wet wraps. These are dressings that keep your baby's skin moist and protected from scratching. Your doctor will refer your baby to a specialist nursing team for help with this treatment.
Wet wraps are only offered for babies who are nine months or older. They're not suitable for larger areas of skin, as the moist cloth can make babies chilly.
What happens if my baby's eczema becomes infected?
If your baby's eczema becomes infected, it won't get better by itself and the usual eczema treatments won't work. Take your baby to your GP as soon as possible. Germs, such as bacteria and viruses, can get into the skin more easily with eczema because the skin barrier is weakened.
Here’s how to tell if your baby’s eczema is infected, and what to do:
Bacterial infections
A bacterial infection will make eczema look redder, or darker, depending on your baby's skin tone. In good light, you may be able to see an orange-tinted shine to the affected areas. As the infection takes hold, these areas may turn oozy, then crusty and yellow.
Your baby may also seem unwell, and develop a fever.
Your baby's bacterial infection can soon be cleared up with antibiotics. Your GP will give you a cream to put on your baby's skin, or drops to put in their mouth, depending on how far the infection has spread. It's important to follow your doctor's instructions and complete the course of antibiotics to make sure your baby recovers fully.
Viral infections
Childhood viral infections, such as chickenpox, molluscum contagiosum, and hand, foot and mouth disease (HFMD) can be worse for babies and children with eczema. Your baby may just need a little extra care to recover from these common illnesses, but always see your doctor if you're worried.
A much more serious, but thankfully rare, illness can be caused by the cold sore virus, herpes simplex. Herpes simplex spreads easily. When it infects eczema it can develop fast into a condition called eczema herpeticum. The signs of eczema herpeticum are:
- Sore-looking, painful patches of eczema that get worse quickly.
- Clusters of fluid-filled blisters that break open, leaving shallow, open sores that may bleed.
- A high temperature and appearing unwell.
Eczema herpeticum is a medical emergency. If you think your baby is affected, see your GP straight away. If it's out of hours, call NHS 111 for urgent advice or take your baby to the accident and emergency department (A&E) of your local hospital.
A doctor will give your baby a course of antiviral medication called aciclovir to treat the infection. This may involve a short stay in hospital, so doctors and nurses there can keep an eye on your baby's treatment and recovery.
Bear in mind that if your baby has mild eczema they are very unlikely to develop eczema herpeticum. The illness is most likely to affect someone with severe eczema.
However, cold sores are common and are highly contagious from the moment they start to tingle to when they heal completely. So it's sensible to be cautious. Don't let anyone with a cold sore, or who thinks they may have one coming on, touch your baby's skin. Be careful if you get one yourself. Don't kiss or share utensils with your baby until your cold sore has disappeared.
Will my baby grow out of eczema?
It's impossible to say for certain, but eczema often does improve or disappear as children grow. Six in 10 children are clear of symptoms by their teenage years.
However for some people eczema is a life-long condition and your baby may always have a tendency to have dry, sensitive skin.

If your baby has erythema toxicum, it will appear as a red, blotchy rash on white skin, sometimes with little spots or small yellow-white pustules. On brown or black skin the rash can be harder to see. It can appear anywhere on your baby's body, apart from the palms of their hands or the soles of their feet.
In spite of the name, erythema toxicum isn't toxic, and shouldn't bother your baby. The rash will usually disappear on its own within a few days or weeks.
What is erythema toxicum?
Erythema toxicum is a harmless blotchy, red or purple rash that affects about half of babies soon after birth, usually in the first couple of days.
The rash appears on the face, neck, upper arms, thighs, and central part of your baby’s body and doesn’t spread to the hands and feet. It will appear more red if your baby has white skin and more purple or deep burgundy if your baby has brown or black skin.
It’s not clear what causes erythema toxicum. One theory is that it happens as your baby’s immune system adjusts to the outside world.
In spite of the name, erythema toxicum is not toxic. It doesn’t mean your baby is ill, or has an allergy. It's unlikely to bother your baby, and it should clear up on its own in a few days to a week, though for a few babies the rash may come and go.
You don’t need to wash your baby’s skin more than usual, and don’t squeeze any of the spots. Just follow your baby’s usual gentle bathing and skincare routine. It won’t be long before your baby’s skin is back to normal.
Some parents like to smooth breastmilk on the spotty areas of their baby’s skin. It’s true that breastmilk can help to fight some baby infections, but there’s no proof it helps with erythema toxicum.
Occasionally, erythema toxicum in babies with dark brown or black skin may be confused with another harmless but rarer rash called transient neonatal pustular melanosis (TNPM).
TNPM affects babies with black or brown skin more than those with white skin. It’s not known what causes it. Unlike erythema toxicum, TNPM spots may spread to the hands and feet.
The spots aren’t sore for your baby, and are usually gone in a couple of weeks. The spots burst easily, though, leaving little flaky ring-shaped marks that may persist for a further few weeks.

Folliculitis happens when your baby's hair follicles become infected. If your baby has it, you'll notice little pus-filled spots around some of their hair follicles. These spots can appear anywhere on your baby's body that grows hair, most likely on their arms, legs, armpits or bottom. Red spots may be less obvious on brown or black skin but they can also look like white-filled bumps.
Most cases of folliculitis will get better on their own within 10 days. Warm cloths (compresses) may help ease symptoms and may help it clear up faster. If your baby's folliculitis doesn't seem to be clearing up within a few days, see your GP. They may prescribe an antibiotic cream to help it clear up faster.
7 tips to care for your baby's skin
As a parent, you will spend a lot of time nuzzling and caressing your baby's soft skin. Find out how to protect your baby's skin from drying out, getting irritated, or becoming damaged with these skin care tips.
7 tips to care for your baby’s skin
#1: Bathe your three times a week. Bathing more frequently may dry out your little one's skin.
#2: Use gentle products without dyes, fragrances, and parabens. This goes for everything that touches your baby's skin:
- soap
- shampoo
- lotion
- laundry detergent
#3: Wash new baby clothes to remove substances that might irritate your baby's skin. Also remove any tags that might scratch newborn skin.
#4: Keep nails short. Babies don't have much control of their limbs, so they can easily scratch themselves with their sharp little nails.
#5: Wipe away drool. The constant presence of saliva on your baby's chin and neck can cause irritation. Gently dab it away with a soft cloth. Try using a bib that you can change when wet.
#6: When in the sun, wear protective clothing and sunscreen. Bring a hat for your baby, choose shade over direct sunlight, and use a mineral-based sunscreen on exposed skin.
#7: Avoid picking at your baby's skin. Picking at bumps or flakes can cause infections or scarring. These things will go away on their own.

Hand, foot and mouth disease (HFMD)
The symptoms of hand, foot and mouth disease (HFMD) include:
- small blister-like sores
- sore throat
- fever
The sores will appear in your baby's mouth and on their hands and feet. They may also spread up your baby's legs and on to their bottom. They can look pink, red, or darker than surrounding skin, depending on your baby’s skin colour. They may be more obvious inside your baby's mouth and on the palms of their hands and soles of their feet. The blisters may be extremely sore.
Hand, foot and mouth disease in babies
Hand, foot and mouth disease (HFMD) is a childhood illness caused by a virus. It's most common in babies and very young children, although adults can get it too. Early symptoms of HFMD include fever, sore throat and generally feeling unwell. Within a few days, your baby may develop mouth ulcers followed by a telltale blistered rash on their hands and feet. Hand, foot and mouth disease is usually a mild illness which gets better on its own within about a week. So long as your baby seems well, they can go to their nursery or childminder while the blisters are healing.
What is hand, foot and mouth disease (HFMD)?
Hand, foot and mouth disease (HFMD) is a mild illness that usually clears up by itself. If your baby has it, you'll see little sores on their hands and feet, and in their mouth, hence the name hand, foot and mouth disease. HFMD is most common in children under four years.
HFMD passes easily from person to person. It spreads quickly in families, and in places where lots of young children play closely together, such as playgroups and nurseries.
Your baby can catch HFMD if someone coughs or sneezes near them, or from contact with traces of poo, saliva, or fluid from the sores.
If your baby catches the disease, they will be most contagious just before the symptoms appear, so it can be hard to prevent in places where babies and children mix.
What causes hand, foot and mouth disease?
HFMD is caused by one of a group of viruses that live in the digestive system (enteroviruses). In the UK, HMFD is usually caused by a coxsackie virus (coxsackie A16) or a related enterovirus (enterovirus 71).
HFMD has nothing to do with foot and mouth disease, which affects farm animals.
What are the symptoms of hand, foot and mouth disease?
The most obvious symptoms are the telltale blisters, but before these appear, your baby may have:
- a sore throat
- a fever
- loss of appetite
After a few days you'll notice the spots:
- Mouth: you'll see red spots on your baby's tongue, and inside their mouth. The spots will turn into larger, yellow-grey blisters rimmed with red.
- Hands and feet: You'll see small, raised red spots on your baby's fingers, on the backs or palms of their hands, on the soles of their feet and on their toes. The spots may then turn into sore, itchy blisters with a grey centre.
Occasionally, the spots spread to the legs, bottom and groin. These look more like a red, bumpy rash than blisters.
The spots may be more difficult to see on black or brown skin, particularly in the early stages. It's best to check inside your baby's mouth and on the palms of their hands and soles of their feet, where the skin is usually lighter.
Your baby may be reluctant to drink or eat because of the mouth sores. If your baby has started solids, they may also go off their food.
How can I care for my baby while they have hand, foot and mouth disease?
It will probably take a week to 10 days for your baby to feel better. By then, their spots should have gone.
In the meantime, your baby will probably be grizzly and hard to settle, but there are things you can do to comfort them:
- If it hurts for your baby to eat or drink, try offering smaller but more frequent feeds of their usual milk. If you're breastfeeding, your baby's mouth blisters won't spread to your nipples. You're probably immune anyway. Formula-fed babies can have extra water, too.
- If your baby has started solid foods, give them soft, easy-to-eat meals, such as mashed potato or soup - nothing spicy or tart, as this could sting their mouth.
- Baby teething gel may relieve your baby’s mouth blisters. Rub some gel on their gums, tongue and the insides of their cheeks where you can see sores. You can also try mouth ulcer gel, but speak to your pharmacist first about the best product for your baby.
- Infant paracetamol or infant ibuprofen may help to relieve pain and reduce fever. You can usually give your baby paracetamol from two months of age. You can usually give ibuprofen from three months of age so long as they weigh at least 5kg (11lb). Check the packet or ask your doctor or pharmacist for advice on how much to give your baby.
After a bath, pat your baby dry, as the affected areas of skin may be tender. Try not to pop any of your baby's blisters, as the fluid is infectious.
If your baby goes to nursery or childcare, keep them at home until they feel better. You don't need to wait until the sores have disappeared to send them back, though your nursery or childminder may have their own policies.
Should I take my baby to the doctor for hand, foot and mouth disease?
You shouldn't need to take your baby to the doctor. HFMD can’t be treated with antibiotics, because it’s a virus. It just needs to run its course, however miserable it is for your baby and you.
Sometimes, though, HFMD causes problems that do need a doctor's advice. Your baby may become dehydrated if HFMD makes it too uncomfortable to drink. Take your baby to the doctor if you spot these signs of dehydration:
- a sunken soft spot on their head
- drowsiness or irritability
- tearless crying
- fewer wet nappies than usual
- sunken eyes
Keep an eye on your baby's other symptoms too. Contact your GP surgery if:
- Your baby has a very high temperature or feels hot and shivery.
- The symptoms do not improve after seven to 10 days, such as the sores not healing or looking infected.
- You are worried about their symptoms.
It's rare for the sores caused by HFMD to become infected (secondary infection), although it can happen if your baby has scratched at them.
Your baby's skin may peel as they recover from the sores. This usually looks worse than it feels for your baby and the sores will heal without leaving a scar. However, if your baby is scratching, keep the rash, and their hands and nails clean, or put mittens or socks over the affected areas.
Occasionally, babies and children shed a fingernail or toenail weeks after the infection has cleared, especially if the blisters were big. This may look alarming to you, but your baby shouldn't be bothered by it. Their nails will grow back by themselves without medical treatment.
Can my baby get hand, foot and mouth disease again?
Yes. Your baby will be immune to the particular strain of virus they’ve had. But, like cold viruses, another strain of virus can come along and set off another bout of HFMD.
You can help to protect your baby against getting HFMD again by being careful with hygiene. Try to stifle coughs and sneezes with a tissue, and throw away tissues after one use. Wash and dry your hands and your baby’s hands often with soap and water. There's no need to use antibacterial soap.
Key times to wash hands to prevent viruses like HFMD include:
- Before and after changing nappies.
- After going to the toilet.
- Before breastfeeding or formula-feeding your baby.
- Before mealtimes, if your baby has started solids.
- After touching used tissues.
I’m pregnant. Will hand, foot and mouth disease harm my unborn baby?
You're probably immune to the various strains of the virus that usually cause HFMD. Even if you do get HFMD, it’s likely to be very mild, and your unborn baby should be unaffected.
However, if you catch HFMD in the weeks before your baby's due, see your midwife or doctor. There's a small chance you could pass the infection to your newborn. It's likely to be a mild infection for your baby too, but it's helpful for your medical and midwifery team to know if there's a chance your baby could become infected.
To protect yourself against HFMD:
- Always wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water after going to the toilet, and after changing or handling nappies. The virus can remain live in your baby's poo for about a month after the sores have cleared up.
- Make sure the toilet and nappy cleaning areas are kept clean.
- Wash soiled bedding or clothing on a hot wash.
- Avoid sharing cups, cutlery or towels.

Heat rash (also known as prickly heat, sweat rash or miliaria) is usually completely harmless. It happens because your baby's sweat glands aren't mature yet, so sweat can build up just under their skin, causing a rash. The rash often looks red on white skin, but may be less obvious on brown or black skin.
The rash is unlikely to bother your baby, though it can sometimes be a bit itchy and uncomfortable.
What is heat rash?
Heat rash - also known as prickly heat, sweat rash or miliaria - is a mild and usually harmless condition that often affects young babies.
It's not contagious, and it usually clears up on its own within a few days. The main way to treat and prevent it is simply to keep your baby cool.
What causes heat rash?
Heat rash is common in babies because their sweat glands are still developing. When your baby gets hot and sweaty, the sweat can build up in his skin instead of coming out through his pores. This can cause tiny patches of swelling, which appear as a rash.
How can I tell if my baby has heat rash?
It can be difficult to tell the difference between heat rash and other common newborn rashes. One obvious clue is if the rash appears when your little one is particularly hot and sweaty.
Heat rash looks like lots of tiny bumps, which can sometimes be a bit red. It can appear anywhere on your little one's body or face. In newborns, it often crops up on the head, face, neck or chest. Older babies may be more prone to getting it in skin folds, such as around the neck, armpits or nappy area.
Heat rash may not bother your baby at all, but it can sometimes be a bit itchy and uncomfortable. It usually clears up within a few hours or days.
Is heat rash serious?
Not usually. In most cases, heat rash is just a minor annoyance, that should soon get better once your baby cools off.
(However, it can be a sign that your baby is too warm. If your baby gets too hot for too long, it can increase the risk of dehydration or heatstroke. If your baby also seems generally unwell, or has symptoms of dehydration, and cooling him down doesn't help, call 111 for urgent medical advice (in Wales call 0845 46 47, and in Northern Ireland call your local GP surgery to find your out-of-hours service).
How can I prevent and treat heat rash?
Your baby's heat rash will probably clear up on its own within a few hours or days. In the meantime, here's what you can do to relieve any itching or discomfort:
- Try to reduce heat and humidity. Move into an airy room or a shady spot. Try using a mini fan if you're out and about in a hot country or in the summer heat. If the weather stays hot at night, open windows and doors to circulate the air.
- Take off his clothes or dress him in cotton. Synthetic fabrics, such as polyester and nylon, trap heat. Opt for natural fibres instead. Where possible, loosen or remove his clothing and give him as much nappy-free time as you can.
- Keep his skin cool. Cool the affected areas directly using cool, wet flannels, or give your baby a tepid bath or shower.
- Keep him hydrated. If your baby's breastfed, offer extra breastfeeds to reduce the risk of dehydration. If he's formula-fed, offer extra drinks of water in a separate bottle or cup. Don't add extra water to your baby's formula, as this can mean he doesn't get all the nutrients he needs.
A note of caution: don't drape a muslin or blanket over your baby's pram to cool him down. This will trap heat, and is likely to make your baby much hotter, rather than cooler. Instead, try to keep your baby's pram in the shade. Check on him often while he's in his pram or pushchair, to make sure he's not getting too warm.
If the rash is bothering your baby, speak to your pharmacist. She may recommend calamine lotion or a moisturiser (emollient) to soothe your baby's skin.
If your baby has particularly bad heat rash, and creams from your pharmacist don't help, see your GP. He may prescribe a mild steroid cream that can help to reduce inflammation and itching, and make your baby feel better.
