If your baby has hives (also known as urticaria or nettle rash), they'll have raised, swollen patches on their skin, which will be very itchy. They can be the same colour as the surrounding skin or have a red tinge, which may not appear on brown and black skin.
Hives often appear in response to some kind of trigger, such as an allergen or a mild infection.
What are hives?
Hives (also known as nettle rash, wheals or urticaria) are raised, swollen, itchy areas on the skin. On white skin the rash may look red. On brown and black skin the colour of the rash might be harder to see. They can appear on any part of your baby's body, usually after contact with some kind of trigger, such as an allergen or illness.
Hives are very common, affecting up to one in five people at some point in their lives. They usually appear suddenly, and go away within a few hours, though they can return. Most cases of hives go away entirely within a few days or weeks, but occasionally they can keep coming back for a year or more.
Although hives can be itchy and uncomfortable for your baby, they're unlikely to cause them any harm. They're also not contagious, so you don't have to worry about your baby passing them on to anyone else.
Why does my baby have hives?
Hives happen when your baby's immune system releases natural chemicals under their skin. This can sometimes happen spontaneously, with no obvious cause. But it's often a response to some kind of trigger.
In babies and young children, up to four in five cases of hives are triggered by an infection, such as a cold or flu.
Other possible triggers for hives in babies include:
- medication, such as antibiotics and ibuprofen
- a sting from a bee, wasp or hornet
- food allergies, particularly to milk, eggs, peanuts, other nuts, soy or wheat
- other allergies, such as to pets, latex, or certain plants
- a physical reaction, for example if your baby gets too hot or cold
How can I treat my baby's hives?
Your baby's hives may go away on their own in a few hours or days. In the meantime, the following tips can help to make them more comfortable:
- If you think your baby's hives may have been triggered by something in their environment, try to remove the trigger if possible.
- Giving your baby a cool bath may help to soothe any itching. A bath that's too cold can be uncomfortable for your little one though, so check it with your elbow first.
- Keep your baby's nails short and clean to protect their skin if they try to scratch. You could also consider using anti-scratch mittens, or putting socks over their hands.
- Ask your pharmacist about calamine lotion, or a soothing emollient cream. These can help to ease any itching or discomfort.
- Heat can sometimes aggravate hives, so try to keep your baby cool, particularly at night. Open doors or windows to allow air to circulate, and use light blankets (or none at all), rather than a heavy sleeping bag.
- If the hives appear around areas where your baby's clothes are tight or rubbing, try dressing them in looser clothing.
If your baby's hives are still bothering them, see your pharmacist. They may recommend a sedating antihistamine that can soothe your baby's symptoms and help your baby get some sleep.
If antihistamines don't help your baby's hives, see your GP. They may recommend a short course of corticosteroids to help your baby feel better. In some cases, they may refer you to a specialist, to make sure that your little one gets the best treatment.
Can hives cause any complications?
Although hives can be itchy and uncomfortable for your baby, they're not usually serious, and they're likely to get better quickly. However, sometimes people with hives can also develop swelling around their hands, feet, eyes, mouth or genitals. This is known as angioedema.
Angioedema also isn't usually serious, and will probably get better by itself within a few days. It's treated in the same way as hives, so any antihistamines or corticosteroids recommended by your GP or pharmacist will also help to treat any swelling.
In rare cases, angioedema associated with hives can progress into a severe allergic reaction, called anaphylaxis. Symptoms can come on very quickly and can be fatal. This is very unlikely to happen to your baby, but it pays to know the symptoms to look out for, just in case.
Call 999 immediately if your baby has hives and develops other symptoms, such as:
- wheezing
- difficulty breathing
- swelling of the lips, tongue, mouth and throat
- a rapid heart rate
- skin that feels cold and clammy
- loss of consciousness
Learn more about anaphylaxis in babies.
Can I prevent my baby from getting hives again?
In many cases, hives will just be a one-off response to a virus or other infection, and you won't need to worry about them coming back. But if your little one keeps getting hives, it may be helpful to keep a diary of the foods they eat, and any other potential triggers they come across. This can help you to work out if there's something in particular that triggers their hives.
If you know what's causing your baby's hives, the best way to prevent them is to avoid the trigger as much as possible. If you suspect that a particular food could be the culprit, speak to your GP before removing the food from their diet. Your GP will be able to help you to make sure that your baby doesn't miss out on any important nutrients as a result.
If it's not obvious what's causing your child's hives, your GP may offer you some tests to try to identify the cause. Or they may refer you to a specialist for further tests and treatment to improve your little one's symptoms.
The good news is that about half of people with recurring hives find that they stop coming back within a year, and four out of five people are better within five years.

Your baby's impetigo will probably first appear as blisters on their face and hands, but it can spread to other parts of their body. The blisters may be reddish at first, although the redness might not appear on brown or black skin.
Once the blisters have burst and dried, a scabby golden brown crust will form. The crusts will gradually heal and won't leave scars.
Impetigo can be itchy and can sometimes be painful. Your baby may also have a temperature and swollen lymph glands in their face or neck.
What is impetigo?
Impetigo is the most common skin infection among babies and young children. It causes distinctive blisters or sores, which can be itchy or uncomfortable for your baby.
The blisters are red on white skin and can be harder to see on brown and black skin.
The infection is caused by bacteria, and is very contagious, but it's unlikely to cause your baby any harm. It usually clears up within a few weeks, and antibiotics can help it clear up faster.
There are two types of impetigo that can affect your baby, and they have slightly different symptoms:
Non-bullous impetigo
This is the most common type of impetigo. It usually begins with sores around your baby's nose and mouth, which can spread to other areas of their face or body.
These sores quickly burst, leaving golden brown crusts that can look a bit like cornflakes stuck to your baby's skin. They usually heal, without scarring, within two or three weeks.
Non-bullous impetigo is unlikely to be painful for your baby, but it may be uncomfortably itchy. Your little one isn't likely to have any other symptoms, but in particularly bad cases, they may develop a fever or swollen glands, and feel generally under the weather.
Bullous impetigo
This type of impetigo is less common, though when it does happen, it often affects newborns and babies less than two years old. It starts with larger blisters (up to 2cm across) around your baby's skin folds – such as elbows, knees, armpits and nappy area - or their face, chest, arms or legs.
The blisters last for about two or three days before bursting, leaving a yellow-brown crust. This gradually heals, without scarring, over the course of about two or three weeks.
Bullous impetigo is more likely to be painful for your baby, so you may notice they're more irritable than usual. If they have this type of impetigo, they'll also more likely to develop other symptoms, such as a fever, swollen glands, diarrhoea, and feeling generally unwell.
How did my baby get impetigo?
The bacteria that cause impetigo are highly contagious, so your baby could have caught it by touching someone who has it, or by sharing toys, clothes or towels with them.
It's particularly easy for your baby to catch impetigo if they have broken skin, for example due to an insect bite, or an existing skin condition such as eczema. It also spreads more easily in hot and humid weather.
How can my baby’s impetigo be treated?
If you think your baby could have impetigo, see your GP. In most cases, they'll prescribe an antibiotic cream to speed up the healing process and help your little one feel better, sooner.
If your baby’s impetigo is severe or widespread, your doctor may prescribe antibiotic liquid for you to give them by mouth. Give your baby the full course of antibiotics, even if their symptoms clear up quickly. This will help to prevent the infection from returning or becoming resistant to the antibiotics.
With antibiotic treatment, your baby's impetigo should clear up within a week to 10 days. If their symptoms don't start to improve within five days of starting treatment, take them back to your GP. They'll check to see whether it's definitely impetigo, and may prescribe a different type of medicine.
Sometimes, impetigo keeps coming back. If this happens to your baby, tell your GP. They may offer to take a swab from your baby's nose, to see if they're carrying a certain type of bacteria. If so, your GP may prescribe an antiseptic cream that you can use around their nose to reduce the risk of impetigo coming back again.
In rare cases, impetigo can develop into a more serious skin condition (cellulitis), or another potentially serious illness such as septicaemia or scarlet fever. If your baby seems to be getting worse, or you have any concerns about their symptoms, call 111 for urgent advice (in Wales call 0845 46 47, and in Northern Ireland call your local GP surgery to find your out-of-hours service).
How can I care for my baby while they have impetigo?
Because impetigo is so infectious, you'll need to keep your baby home from nursery or childcare. They can usually go back after they've been treated with antibiotics for 48 hours, but check with your childcare provider first.
If your baby isn't able to take antibiotics, they'll need to stay home until all the sores or blisters have dried out and crusted over.
While you're waiting for your baby's impetigo to clear up, the following tips will help to promote healing and reduce the risk of the infection spreading:
- Keep the sores clean and dry by regularly washing with soap and warm water, then gently patting dry with a clean cloth.
- Cover the sores with loose clothing or bandages to prevent your baby scratching and reduce the risk of the infection spreading.
- Avoid touching the sore areas as much as possible. Wash your hands often, particularly before and after applying any antibiotic cream, and after any time you accidentally touch the sores.
- Try to discourage your baby from scratching their sores, and keep their nails trimmed and clean to reduce any damage to their skin when they do scratch. You could also consider using anti-scratch mittens.
- Keep your baby’s flannel, towels, sheets, clothes and soft toys separate from those used by other family members. Wash them on a hot wash after your baby has used them
- Wipe down plastic or wooden toys with detergent and warm water after your baby has touched them.
Following these hygiene measures will help to protect the rest of your family while your baby has impetigo. In most cases, your little one will be back to their normal self within a week to 10 days of starting treatment.

More than half of all babies develop a yellowish tinge to their skin in the first few days after birth. If your baby has brown or black skin, you are more likely to notice a yellow tinge to the white of their eyes, or on the palms of their hands or soles of their feet.
If your baby was born full term, it will usually take a week or two for their skin and eye colour to return to normal. It may take a bit longer if they were born early.
What is jaundice?
Jaundice happens when too much of a natural chemical called bilirubin builds up in your baby's body. Jaundice usually appears two or three days after birth.
Bilirubin is made when red blood cells reach the end of their life and break down. Newborns tend to have high levels of bilirubin because they have extra red blood cells. As well as this, their young livers are less efficient at processing bilirubin. It's all part of adjusting to life outside the womb (uterus).
If your baby has white skin, jaundice will make their skin look yellow. If your baby has black or brown skin, the yellowness will show more clearly in the whites of their eyes and on their palms and soles of their feet.
As bilirubin levels rise above normal, the yellowness of jaundice moves downwards from your baby's head and face, before spreading to their chest and tummy. For some babies, the yellowness reaches their arms and legs.
Jaundice affects more than half of all healthy babies in the first week of life. It is even more common among premature babies.
As long as your baby is otherwise healthy, jaundice won't harm them and will go away within a week or two. By the time your baby is two weeks old, their liver is better able to process bilirubin, so jaundice goes.
How can I tell if my baby has jaundice?
In a well-lit room, gently press your fingers on your baby's nose or forehead. If there's a yellow tinge to their skin as the pressure is released, tell your midwife or doctor. If your baby has dark skin, check for yellowness in the whites of their eyes or gums.
Another way you can tell if your baby has jaundice is by comparing the colour of the back of their hands with the colour of their face.
You may also notice that your baby:
- Is sleepy and floppy, and doesn't feed well.
- Has a higher-pitched cry than other babies.
- Does dark yellow wees and pale poos. Healthy wee is colourless to pale yellow and normal baby poos are yellow or orange. Jaundiced babies' poo is pale because not much bilirubin reaches the digestive system.
Always tell your midwife, health visitor or doctor if your baby has jaundice. They will check your baby's overall health and advise you whether they need treatment.
Is my baby likely to get jaundice?
Your baby is more likely to develop jaundice if:
- They were premature.
- They have an older brother or sister who needed treating for jaundice.
- You had an assisted birth with ventouse or forceps, as babies with bruising are more likely to get jaundice.
- You opted for delayed cord clamping. Your baby benefits from having extra placental blood, but it does mean they'll have more blood cells to break down.
Breastfeeding your baby exclusively can increase their chances of developing jaundice. To help clear the jaundice, breastfeed them often. The advice to breastfeed your baby as much as possible may sound confusing, but it does help to clear jaundice. The more your baby feeds, the more often they'll poo. Each time your baby poos, they get rid of a bit more bilirubin from their body.
Your baby may poo each time you breastfeed them in the early weeks. You may need to wake your baby to feed them frequently if they are very sleepy.
Massaging your baby’s tummy every day, in a clockwise circular motion, can help move your baby's poo through her system, and so help the jaundice to clear.
You don't need to give your baby formula milk or water instead of breastmilk. Breastmilk is best for your baby, for many reasons.
Is jaundice serious?
Jaundice on its own is very rarely serious. It usually starts a couple of days after birth and clears up without any treatment within a couple of weeks. However, occasionally, jaundice can be a sign of another illness, and this can be signalled if the jaundice doesn't follow the usual pattern.
Call your doctor if:
- your baby becomes jaundiced within 24 hours of birth
- your baby becomes jaundiced for the first time when they're more than seven days old
- your baby's jaundice lasts for more than 21 days if your baby was premature
- your baby's jaundice lasts for more than 14 days if your baby was full term
The following underlying conditions can cause jaundice:
- An underactive thyroid gland (hypothyroidism), where the thyroid gland doesn't produce enough hormones.
- Incompatible blood groups between a mum and their baby. These different blood types may have mixed during the pregnancy or birth. For example, if the mum has rhesus-negative blood and the baby has rhesus-positive blood.
- A urinary tract infection (UTI).
- A blockage or problem in the bile ducts and gallbladder. These organs create and transport bile, which helps to digest fats.
- An inherited enzyme deficiency called glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. G6PD deficiency is more common in people of African, Asian or Mediterranean descent. If you have a family history of G6PD deficiency, tell your midwife or doctor so they can monitor your baby's symptoms closely.
There is also an extremely rare complication of untreated newborn jaundice called kernicterus. Kernicterus only affects one baby in 100,000. It can cause long-term problems, such as cerebral palsy, hearing loss, learning difficulties, and eye and tooth problems. As well as severe jaundice, kernicterus causes a baby to feed very poorly and go floppy, like a rag doll.
How will I know if my baby needs treatment for jaundice?
Whether or not your baby needs hospital treatment will depend on their bilirubin levels. Your doctor can check their bilirubin levels in two ways:
- Using a small device called a bilirubinometer. This beams light on to your baby's skin. It works out how much bilirubin is in their body by checking how the light bounces off or is absorbed by their skin.
- By taking a small blood sample via a heel prick test. It's only a small, quick prick, so it shouldn't upset your baby too much. The level of bilirubin in the blood can then be measured.
Usually, a bilirubinometer will give all the information your doctor needs to decide treatment, if any.
Your baby should only need a blood test if:
- they were born prematurely
- they've developed jaundice within their first 24 hours of birth
- their bilirubin levels are especially high.

If your baby’s bilirubin levels are rising, or already high, they may need treatment in hospital, possibly in a special care baby unit. There are different levels of treatment, depending on how jaundiced your baby is:
Conventional phototherapy
Your baby will lie on a bed under a light that emits rays at a certain wavelength. The light helps to break down the excess bilirubin so that their liver can get rid of it. It's not like sunlight, so it won't burn their skin, but they may develop a temporary and harmless rash afterwards.
A nurse will put special glasses or goggles on your baby to protect their eyes.
Phototherapy is a very safe treatment, but it may make your baby warm and dehydrated. Hospital staff check your baby's temperature during the treatment and will stop it every three or four hours to give them a break.
Each break usually lasts about half an hour, and it's a chance for you to feed and cuddle your baby, and change their nappy. Your doctor or nurse may check your baby's nappies for signs of dehydration.
Breastfeeding your baby at breaks in the treatment is the best way to keep them hydrated, and hospital staff should support you to do this.
However, if your doctor is concerned your baby is becoming dehydrated they may ask to give your baby extra fluids via a drip. Most of the time, babies having phototherapy don't need this.
Intensified phototherapy
If your baby's jaundice doesn’t improve quickly enough your doctor will recommend intensified phototherapy. This involves continuous phototherapy, with no breaks for feeding. It uses a stronger light source, or more than one light source.
Your baby will need feeding through a very fine, soft tube that the doctor will pass through her nose and into her tummy. Ideally, you'll be able to express enough milk to keep your baby going through the treatment.
Fibreoptic therapy
Your baby will be wrapped in a special blanket containing fibreoptics, which shines little lights directly on to their skin. You can still cuddle and feed your baby, so it is better for bonding. Fibreoptic treatment may be offered first if your baby is premature.
Although light is an effective treatment for jaundiced babies, don't try to treat your baby yourself by exposing them to sunlight. Sunlight can damage your baby's fragile skin and make them too hot. Light treatment offered in hospitals is very safe and effective.
Exchange transfusion
If your baby has extremely high levels of bilirubin in their blood, perhaps caused by an underlying health problem, they may need an exchange transfusion. This involves some of your baby’s blood gradually being replaced with suitable blood from a donor.
Your baby will have close care to make sure they stay well during the treatment, which may take several hours. The new blood won't contain any bilirubin, so the bilirubin levels in your baby's blood will fall.
If your baby does need to spend some time in hospital, find out how to care for them in the neonatal unit.

Sometimes, a tick bite can lead to lyme disease. This is a serious bacterial infection that needs prompt treatment. If your baby is bitten by a tick, look out for a spreading rash or ring around the site of the bite. The rash may be flat, or slightly raised. It may look pink or red on white skin and brown, black or purple on brown and black skin, similar to a bruise.
If you spot this, take your baby to your GP.
I think my baby has a tick. How can I remove it?
A tick is a small, round insect with no wings. Although they usually live on animals, they can sometimes bite humans, too. They're most common in wild areas such as forests and woodland, but can also appear in parks and gardens.
Your baby probably won't notice if she's bitten by a tick, as the bites are usually painless. If she has been bitten, the tick will stay on her skin for up to a week. However, ticks can be hard to spot, as they're often as small as a poppy seed.
Tick bites are usually harmless, but they can sometimes spread a serious illness known as lyme disease. So it's a good idea to check your baby for ticks regularly, especially after spending time with her outside. You're most likely to spot one around her hairline and scalp.
If you notice a tick on your baby, try to remove it as soon as possible:
- Use a pair of fine-tipped tweezers to grab the tick as close to your baby’s skin as possible.
- Gently pull straight up until all parts of the tick are removed. Take care not to crush the tick's body, as this could make your baby's bite worse.
- After removing the tick, wash your hands with soap and water, and apply an antiseptic cream to the skin around the bite.
Don’t try to get the tick out by using petroleum jelly, alcohol, or a lit match, as these won’t work.
Ideally, once you've removed the tick, put it in a sealed container and send it to the government's tick recording scheme. This helps to keep track of lyme disease in the UK. If that's not possible, crush the tick using a hard object, being careful not to get any of its blood on your skin. Then just flush it down the loo, or wrap it in sticky tape and pop it in the bin.
If you’re worried about removing the tick yourself, take your baby to your GP or local walk-in centre. A doctor or nurse can remove the tick from your baby’s skin.
A tick bite is unlikely to cause any problems for your baby, but keep an eye on her as it heals. If she develops flu-like symptoms, or a red rash or ring forms around the tick bite and starts to spread, take her to the GP. It could be a sign of lyme disease, which can be serious if untreated, but will usually clear up with a course of antibiotics.

If your baby has measles, their first symptoms can include:
- fever
- runny nose
- sneezing
- cough
- sore, red, swollen eyes
- small white spots in their mouth
Two to four days after these symptoms start, a blotchy rash will develop on your baby's face and behind the ears before spreading to the rest of the body.
The rash looks brown or red on white skin. On brown and black skin, the rash can be harder to see, although it may appear as darker than the skin.
While most babies and children recover from measles without any complications, measles can lead to serious problems if it spreads to other parts of the body, such as the lungs or brain.

Measles in babies
Measles is a highly infectious disease that causes flu-like symptoms and a rash. It's caused by a virus that spreads very easily through coughs and sneezes. Measles can be a serious illness, especially for babies and young children, but it can be prevented by the MMR vaccination. Find out why measles can sometimes be serious, and learn about the signs and symptoms of the disease.
Is my baby at risk of getting measles?
Your baby has an extremely low risk of measles if you have them immunised with the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. After two doses of the MMR about 99 per cent of people are protected against measles.
When your baby is about one year old, you'll be offered the MMR as part of their routine immunisations. A second dose (booster) will be offered when your baby is three years and four months old, or soon after.
If your baby hasn't had the MMR, they do have a small chance of catching measles. Cases of the disease have risen because fewer people are taking up the MMR. This may be because of claims linking the vaccine to autism. But these claims have been shown to be untrue. Be assured that the MMR vaccine is completely safe.
The UK was recognised by the World Health Organization (WHO) for eliminating measles. But now cases are rising, it has lost its measles-free status. Even so, it's still rare for babies to get measles, and any outbreaks of the disease tend to stay local.
How is measles spread?
The measles virus spreads very easily. When an infected person sneezes or coughs, tiny droplets carrying the virus spray into the air. The droplets stay active for a few hours in the air, or on a surface.
Nearly everyone who comes into contact with the virus catches it if they don't have immunity to it. If your baby breathes in the droplets or touches something contaminated by the droplets, they are very likely to get measles.
Being in the same room for at least 15 minutes with someone who has measles is enough to expose your baby to the virus. This could be a situation where you don't realise there's someone with measles nearby, such as in a doctor's surgery waiting area, or at the accident and emergency department of a hospital.
Babies, children and pregnant women who are not immune are all at risk of becoming seriously ill if they get measles.
What are the symptoms of measles?
Before a rash appears, the first symptoms may seem like a standard cold, with:
- a fever
- a runny or blocked nose
- a cough
- sore, red, sticky eyes
This stage can last for a few days to a week. The first sign that your baby has measles, and not a cold, is small, grey-white spots in their mouth. You can check for by looking inside your baby's cheeks and gently pulling down their bottom lip. The spots may look like grains of salt.
Between two days and four days after early symptoms appear, the measles rash appears. The rash is blanching at first, which means it fades if you press it with a glass tumbler. On white skin, the rash is red, growing brown after a few days. The measles rash is harder to see on brown or black skin.
The rash starts on your baby's face and behind their ears, before spreading from the neck down to the rest of their body. It doesn't usually spread to the palms of the hand or soles of the feet. As the rash appears, your baby's fever may rise as high as 40 degrees C.
The spots may be raised and as they spread, they can join up and look blotchy. The rash will last for about five days.
Along with the rash, your baby is likely to:
- be tired and irritable
- have muscle aches and pains
- go off feeds
- have a cough, which can disturb their sleep.
What if my baby's exposed to measles before they've had the MMR?
Call your GP or NHS 111 for advice urgently. Don't go to your surgery without booking an appointment, and don't take your baby to a walk-in clinic. Measles is so infectious that your doctor will want to prioritise seeing your baby in the safest way to contain any spread.
Measles is a notifiable disease, which means the government considers it a risk to public health. Your GP has a legal duty to report suspected measles cases to the authorities.
Treatments for babies work best within the first three days of exposure to measles. So the sooner you get medical help, the better. Your doctor may call your local hospital to see if your baby should be admitted for treatment.
The type of treatment depends on your baby's age:
If your baby is younger than six months
At six months or younger, your baby is too young to have the MMR. But your doctor can give your baby an injection of a substance called human normal immunoglobin (HNIG). HNIG gives your baby a short-term boost of measles antibodies, which can help to make symptoms less severe.
If your baby is between six and eight months
The type of treatment depends on how close your baby has come to the virus:
- Your baby should have HNIG if you live with someone who has measles. HNIG is a better treatment for babies of this age who are at the highest risk of catching the disease.
- Your baby should have the MMR if there's a chance they've been exposed to measles, but they haven’t come into direct contact with the disease.
If your baby is nine months or older
Your doctor will give your baby the standard MMR vaccine, ideally within three days of exposure.
Even if your baby has had measles, or an early dose of the MMR vaccine, they will still need to be immunised at one year, in line with the childhood vaccination programme.
How should I care for my baby with measles?
The best you can do is keep your baby comfortable as the illness runs its course.
Measles is a virus, so it can't be treated with antibiotics. Your baby should get better within a week or so.
Here’s what you can do to make your baby more comfortable, and help them get better:
- Make sure your baby gets plenty of rest.
- Encourage your baby to drink . Offer plenty of breastfeeds. If your baby is formula-fed, offer extra drinks of cooled, boiled water. You could also try an iced lolly if your baby is old enough.
- Give your baby the correct dose of infant paracetamol or infant ibuprofen to ease a fever and any aches and pains.
- If your baby has sore eyes, use cotton wool soaked in warm water gently to wipe away any crusting.
Keep your baby at home and away from other children or pregnant women for at least four days after they develop the rash.
Your baby's rash should fade after about a week, but they may continue to have a cough for a week or so after that.
Can measles cause any complications?
Most babies and children recover from measles without any complications. However, babies under one year are particularly vulnerable.
Common complications of measles include:
- diarrhoea
- ear infections
- chest infections such as bronchitis, croup, or pneumonia.
Common complications can turn serious, because your baby's immune system is weakened during a measles infection. Keep a close eye on your baby. If they seem to find breathing painful or difficult, or cough up blood, call 999 for an ambulance, or go to the accident and emergency (A&E) department of your local hospital. Your baby could have pneumonia that needs hospital treatment.
A serious complication is a febrile seizure or fit. If this happens to your baby, call an ambulance, or go to A&E.
Rarely, measles can also infect the brain and nervous system, leading to the very serious conditions meningitis and encephalitis. These are medical emergencies. If your baby has a rash that doesn't fade, seems floppy or different from normal, call an ambulance.
Read more about meningitis, including which symptoms to look out for.

Meningitis is a serious infection that can develop very quickly. The most distinctive feature is a rash that doesn't disappear when a glass is rolled over it.
On white skin the rash usually starts as small, red pinpricks before spreading quickly and turning into red or purple blotches. The rash may not be as obvious on brown and black skin. Check paler areas of your baby's body, such as the soles of the feet, the palms and the tummy. The rash doesn't always appear, and when it does, the infection is usually already advanced.
Earlier symptoms may include:
- fever
- cold hands and feet
- vomiting
- confusion
- breathing quickly
- muscle and joint pain
- Pale, mottled or blotchy skin
- headache
- a stiff neck
If you suspect your baby may have meningitis, see a doctor straight away: don't wait.
Meningitis in babies (0 to 12 months)
Meningitis is one of the most worrying illnesses for parents of babies and young children. Although meningitis infections are rare, when they do happen they can be serious. You can protect your baby against meningitis by making sure they have all their routine vaccinations. You can also learn to spot the signs of a meningitis infection, and know when to get medical help quickly for your baby. Read on to find out more.
What is meningitis?
Meningitis is when the membranes that surround and protect the brain and spinal cord become inflamed and swollen. This usually happens because the membranes, called the meninges, have become infected from bacteria or a virus.
The inflammation can then cause damage to the brain or nerves. It can also cause blood poisoning, known as septicaemia. Meningitis develops quickly and can be very serious if it isn't treated swiftly.
What is the difference between bacterial and viral meningitis?
Viral meningitis is caused by a virus and bacterial meningitis caused by bacteria. They have similar symptoms but bacterial meningitis is usually more serious. However, it is also rarer, thanks to the childhood vaccination programme.
Viral meningitis often doesn't need treatment. The flu-like symptoms may be unpleasant, but they're likely to go away after about seven to 10 days.
Bacterial meningitis is the most dangerous type because the bacteria can spread throughout the bloodstream, and this causes septicaemia. If it isn’t treated quickly, septicaemia can lead to permanent disabilities and even be life-threatening. It's septicaemia that causes the meningitis rash of red or purple spots that don't fade under pressure.
Which vaccines protect my baby against meningitis?
The following vaccines protect your baby against the main bacterial and viral infections that may lead to meningitis:
- MenB, offered when your baby is two months, four months and one year old. This protects against meningococcal bacteria type B.
- Hib, at two months, three months and four months. This protects against Haemophilus influenzae type B bacteria.
- MenC, combined with a Hib booster, at one year. This protects against meningococcal bacteria type C.
- PCV, at three months and a booster at one year. This protects against pneumococcal bacteria.
MMR, at one year. This protects against the three viruses that cause measles, mumps and rubella.
How does meningitis spread?
The bacteria and viruses that may lead to meningitis usually spread through coughs and sneezes. Many people are infectious because they carry the germs in their noses and throats unknowingly without becoming ill. In fact, your baby is unlikely to catch meningitis directly from someone who is ill with it.
It's still not fully understood why common germs develop into a meningitis infection for some people and not others. We do know that babies and children under five are more vulnerable to meningitis, especially from meningococcal infections. That's why you will be offered the MenB vaccination, along with the other vaccines that help to protect your baby in their first year.
Catching coughs and sneezes in a tissue, washing your hands and keeping surfaces clean makes sense too. These basic hygiene rules reduce the chance of germs spreading to your baby.
How can I tell if my baby has meningitis?
At first, it may seem like your baby has a cold, tummy bug or flu. Having a fever, or going off feeds are typical of many common illnesses but they can also be signs of meningitis.
The following signs of meningitis can vary from baby to baby, and can appear in any order, so don't wait to check them off before getting medical help if you're worried:
- A high fever, though your baby's hands and feet may feel cold. If your baby is less than three months old their body temperature may drop, or they may not develop a fever.
- High-pitched crying, unlike your baby's usual crying.
- Irritability. Your baby won't respond to smiles and chats as normal.
- Extreme sleepiness. Your baby may be hard to wake, or, if they're awake, have a staring expression.
- Fast breathing, or difficulty breathing. Your baby may make odd, grunting noises.
- A rash of red or purple spots that look like pin pricks and don't fade when you press a glass tumbler against them. If your baby has brown or black skin the spots may be harder to see, so check your baby's palms, the soles of their feet, and the roof of their mouth.
- Refusal to feed and vomiting.
- A bulging, or tight-feeling soft spot (fontanelle) on the top of the head.
- Pale skin. If your baby has dark brown or black skin, gently pull down their bottom eyelid to see if it looks pale rather than pink.
- Unusual movements. Your baby may be very floppy, feel stiff, or make jerky movements. Sometimes meningitis can cause fits (seizures).
The early signs of bacterial meningitis, the most dangerous type, can be hard to spot. If it's bacterial meningitis, though, your baby will become seriously ill quickly.
You know your baby best, so if you're concerned, trust your instincts and call 999 or take your baby to your nearest accident and emergency department (A&E or ED). When it comes to suspected meningitis, it's safest to have a doctor check your baby as soon as possible.
How will I know if my baby's rash is the meningitis rash?
Use the glass test. Press the side of a clear drinking glass on the spots. A meningitis rash doesn't fade. It's called a non-blanching rash.
The rash happens when toxins from bacteria that cause meningitis spread to blood vessels (septicaemia), damaging them and causing blood to leak. This leaked blood looks like pinprick red spots on the skin. As the leaks get bigger, the spots can become larger red or purple blotches, like bruises, and blood blisters.
A rash is a sign that the illness is severe and your baby needs urgent medical help. Call 999 for an ambulance or go to A&E if you think your baby has the meningitis rash.
How is meningitis diagnosed?
Suspected meningitis is a medical emergency, so it's usually diagnosed once your baby is in hospital. A hospital team led by a paediatrician will work quickly through checks and tests to tell whether your baby has viral or bacterial meningitis.
The doctor may give your baby antibiotics straight away before confirming what type of meningitis it is. This is because having antibiotics as soon as possible is the best way to help your baby recover from bacterial meningitis.
The doctor will take a sample of your baby's blood and may also need a sample of fluid from your baby's spine. This is called cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and it flows in the membranes of the brain, called meninges. Doctors can check from the blood and CSF samples whether harmful bacteria have spread within the bloodstream and meninges.
To take a CSF sample the doctor or a specialist nurse will insert a fine, hollow needle between the bones of your baby's lower spine to collect a little fluid. This is called a lumbar puncture.
The lumbar puncture may be a little uncomfortable for your baby but it shouldn't hurt. The team carrying it out are highly skilled at ensuring your baby stays well throughout. They may give your baby a calming medicine to help the procedure go smoothly.
It can be distressing for you to watch your baby having a lumbar puncture, however much you know it's for the best. Hospital staff may suggest you step out of the room while they work. It should all be over in about 45 minutes, and your baby will be in good hands while you're outside. The results from the CSF sample test may be back in a couple of hours.
The doctor may also request a CT scan of your baby's brain to check for swelling. A CT scanner is a type of x-ray. It uses the lowest possible level of radiation to take a picture of inside your baby's brain. If you want to be in the room with your baby while the scan is happening, staff will give you a lead apron to wear to protect you from radiation.
CT scans are only used when necessary to help doctors decide the best treatment.
What is the treatment for meningitis?
Your baby's treatment will depend on what type of meningitis they have:
Bacterial meningitis
Your baby will have antibiotics via a drip into a vein. A drip means your baby gets regular, accurate doses of medication. If your baby is seriously unwell, hospital staff may take them to the intensive care unit for closer monitoring and swifter treatment. Your baby may also need:
- Fluids via a drip to prevent dehydration.
- Oxygen through a face mask to help with breathing.
Your baby may need to stay in hospital for at least a week, and likely longer. The length of the stay will depend on how ill your baby is and which strain of bacteria has caused the meningitis.
Viral meningitis
Your baby will just need rest and care to recover. Your baby may have headaches, be grizzly and tired, and reluctant to feed. You can help your baby by:
- Encouraging them to take small, frequent feeds of milk.
- Giving them the correct dose of infant paracetamol or infant ibuprofen to ease headaches.
- Keeping your home calm and quiet so your baby can rest more easily.
Your baby should get better in a week to 10 days. However, if you think your baby is getting worse rather than better, call your doctor. Very rarely, the viruses that cause meningitis can cause other illnesses.
Can newborn babies get meningitis?
Yes, it's called neonatal meningitis when babies develop it in their first month. Meningitis in newborns is very rare. Fewer than one in 2,000 babies develop neonatal bacterial meningitis in the UK each year.
Neonatal meningitis can be caused by a virus, but it's usually caused by bacteria. The main types of bacteria that lead to neonatal meningitis are:
- group B streptococcus (GBS)
- Escherichia coli (E. coli)
Like the germs that cause meningitis in older babies and children, these two bacterial strains are common and only very rarely result in meningitis. Both can pass to a baby during birth, in most cases without causing any harm.
Babies born prematurely and babies born with a low birth weight are more vulnerable to neonatal meningitis. These babies are carefully monitored after birth, so hospital staff will be watching out for any signs of infection.
The signs of neonatal meningitis are similar to those for older babies, except your newborn may have a normal or low temperature. Neonatal meningitis can be difficult to diagnose, though. If you are at all worried about your newborn, and they don't seem well, trust your instincts and get immediate medical help.
Neonatal meningitis is treated with antibiotics, and many newborns who receive treatment recover well. However, about half of newborns who've contracted meningitis may experience longer-term effects. The disease can damage the nervous system, affecting hearing, vision and speech.

Milia are tiny, slightly raised spots that may appear on your baby's face, usually across their nose, cheeks, chin, forehead, or around their eyes. They can also crop up on your baby's chest.
Milia are very common in newborn babies. They're caused by blocked pores, and are completely harmless for your baby.
It’s normal for newborns to develop spots as their delicate skin adjusts to life in the outside world. Spots vary and may look like pimples, acne, or a rash. Usually, they’re harmless and soon go away. But occasionally a rash may mean your baby is unwell. Find out what’s causing your baby’s spots, whether you need to treat them, and when to call the doctor.
Why is my newborn’s face covered in pimples?
Your baby is likely to have a condition called milia, which is common in newborns and nothing to worry about. Your baby may have milia at birth or soon after. If your baby was born prematurely, milia may appear later than this.
You’ll see tiny raised spots, usually sprinkled across your baby’s nose, cheeks, forehead or around the eyes. The spots may look white or yellow, depending on your baby’s skin colour.
Milia happens when a protein called keratin gets trapped under your baby’s skin, forming tiny cysts. Keratin is found naturally in your baby’s skin and helps protect the outer layer.
Milia spots clear up on their own in a few weeks and won’t leave any blemishes.

Molluscum contagiosum appears as small, raised, dome-shaped spots. They're typically pink or red on white skin or a beige colour on brown and black skin. Each spot has a dimple in the middle.
The spots can appear anywhere on your child's body, often in the armpits, behind the knees or around their nappy area. They shouldn't be painful for your little one, though they can sometimes be uncomfortably itchy.
Molluscum contagiosum (water warts) in children ages one to five
Molluscum contagiosum (water warts) is a common skin infection that causes spots to appear on your child's skin. It's usually harmless and your child's unlikely to have any other symptoms. While your GP is unlikely to recommend any treatment, it’s a good idea to get a diagnosis, so they can rule out any other skin conditions.
What is molluscum contagiosum?
Molluscum contagiosum, or water warts, is a mild infection that causes raised spots to appear on your child's skin. It often affects young children, particularly between the ages of one and four. It's usually harmless, and will probably get better on its own within about 18 months.
A virus (molluscum contagiosum virus or MCV) causes the spots so it can be passed from person to person. However, your little one will still be able to go to nursery or preschool as normal while they have it.
What are the symptoms of molluscum contagiosum?
The main – and usually only – symptom of molluscum contagiosum is small, raised, dome-shaped spots. They typically appear flesh-coloured, white, pink or brown, depending on skin colour.
You're most likely to notice these on your child's chest, tummy, back, armpits, behind their knees or in the nappy area, though they can appear anywhere on the body.
There can be up to 30 spots at any one time. Each spot is quite small (usually about 2mm-5mm across). One way to tell if it's molluscum contagiosum is to look for a tell-tale dimple in the middle of each spot.
The spots shouldn't be painful for your child, and they are unlikely to have any other symptoms. In some cases, though, the spots can be uncomfortably itchy, or you may notice dry and cracked skin surrounding them.
The spots usually clear up altogether within about 18 months. However, during this time it's not unusual for new spots to develop elsewhere , as your child still has the virus in their system. They can also transfer by skin-to-skin contact, for example from the side of the chest to the inside of the arm.
Sometimes, the spots can become infected, making them swollen and painful. You can reduce the risk of this happening by encouraging your child to avoid scratching or squeezing their spots.
If your child has a weakened immune system, they may have more spots than usual (over 100), and they may appear larger than normal. In this case, your GP will be able to advise you about the best treatment for your little one.
What’s the best way to treat molluscum contagiosum?
Your GP won’t usually recommend treatment for molluscum contagiosum, because the spots almost always clear up by themselves. However, it's still a good idea to visit your GP, just so they can confirm what's causing the spots, and check for any signs of infection.
If the spots are very itchy, your GP can prescribe a mild corticosteroid cream to help your little one feel better. If there's any sign of infection, they may prescribe an antibiotic to help clear it up.
In rare cases, if the spots are particularly bad, your GP may refer you to a dermatologist, who can offer treatments such as freezing the spots (cryotherapy), cutting the spots off (curettage), or using heat or chemicals to remove them. However, these treatments don't always work, and they can be painful for your child and increase the risk of scarring .
In most cases, the spots shouldn't bother your child, or cause them any problems at all. In these cases, your GP will probably recommend that you just follow the hygiene steps below to help prevent the spots from spreading while you wait for them to clear up.
How does molluscum contagiosum spread?
The spots are caused by a virus, which can be passed from person to person. Your child may have caught it by touching someone who has molluscum contagiosum, or by sharing items such as towels, flannels or clothes with them.
Fortunately, although the spots can pass from person to person, they're not usually very contagious. This means that your child can still go to school as usual while they have it, and enjoy their usual activities, including swimming.
Nonetheless, it's a good idea to take some basic hygiene precautions while your child has molluscum contagiosum, to help prevent it spreading to the rest of the family:
- Avoid squeezing or scratching the spots, and encourage your child to do the same. If the spots are itchy, ask your GP for a cream to soothe them.
- Where possible, keep the spots covered with loose clothing.
- If you're taking your child to a swimming pool, you can use a waterproof bandage to cover the spots.
- Don’t let your child share clothes, towels, flannels or baths with anyone else until the last spot has disappeared.
Will molluscum contagiosum cause scarring?
Fortunately, molluscum contagiosum doesn't usually cause scarring, unless the spots become infected, or have been treated in some way. To reduce the risk of infection, don't squeeze or scratch the spots, and encourage your child to do the same.

Mouth ulcers are sores that can appear anywhere in the mouth, most often on the inside of the cheek or lips. They usually look white or pale yellow, though the area around them may look red or swollen.
Your baby may just get the one ulcer, or several at once. They're not usually very painful, though they can be uncomfortable for your little one.
Your baby may have got an ulcer from accidently biting their cheek or lip, or perhaps a sharp piece of food cut your baby's mouth a little. Tiredness can also trigger ulcers.
Mouth ulcers aren't contagious, and they usually clear up on their own within a week or two. In the meantime, a mouth ulcer can make eating uncomfortable for your baby, so try feeding them softer foods.
Brushing your baby's teeth extra carefully with a soft toothbrush will also help. See your GP if the ulcer lasts for more than three weeks, keeps coming back, or seems to be very painful for your baby.
Find out about other baby mouth and teeth problems, including thrush and teething

Nappy rash causes a puffy rash around your baby's genitals, bottom, and the folds of their thighs. The rash can sometimes look pimply, and may feel warm to the touch. Your baby may often get nappy rash during their first year, and wetness is the main cause, though thrush can also contribute. On black or brown skin, the affected area may lighten. This usually clears up within a few weeks, but in severe cases it can take months or sometimes years to return to the usual skin colour.
If your baby's bottom is looking red and sore, chances are they have nappy rash. While it can sometimes be uncomfortable for your baby, it's usually fairly easy to treat, and a few simple steps can help prevent it from flaring up again.
How common is nappy rash?
Nappy rash is very common. In fact, it’s thought that up to one in three babies has nappy rash at any given time.
Although it can happen at any age while your baby is in a nappy, they’re most likely to have it between the ages of six months and 18 months. Nappy rash is less common in newborns.
What does nappy rash look like?
If your baby has nappy rash, you'll know it. The skin around their nappy area could be:
- red and inflamed (this symptom might not be as noticeable on black or brown skin)
- spotty
- hot to the touch
- shiny
If the rash persists, small blisters or scales may develop.
Nappy rash can affect your baby's genitals, the inside of their thighs, and their bottom. It may begin as a few small patches that spread over the course of several nappy changes, or it may seem to appear quite suddenly.
Mild nappy rash may not bother your baby too much. But if it’s feeling sore, you may notice them crying after they do a wee or when you’re changing their nappy, or they may just seem generally out of sorts.
What are the causes of nappy rash?
Even the most absorbent nappy will leave some moisture on your baby’s skin. This contact with wee or poo is the main cause of nappy rash as it softens and weakens the outer layer of your baby’s skin. A baby left in a wet or soiled nappy for too long is more likely to develop nappy rash.
However, nappy rash can also affect babies with particularly sensitive skin, even if they have frequent, fresh nappies. A nappy that rubs against your baby’s skin can also cause it to become irritated.
Other factors can also increase the likelihood of your baby developing nappy rash. These include:
Diarrhoea
It’s not unusual for babies with diarrhoea to get nappy rash. That’s because the substances in poo that can irritate your baby’s skin, called enzymes, are more active in runny poo than in healthy poo.
Antibiotics
Nappy rash is sometimes caused by thrush, a fungal infection. Taking antibiotics makes thrush more likely. So if you have to give your baby antibiotics, they may be more prone to nappy rash until they finish the course.
Oral thrush
It’s also possible for your baby to have fungal nappy rash even if they aren’t taking antibiotics. In some cases, babies with oral thrush pass the fungus through their digestive system and into their poo, infecting the nappy area.
Allergies
Nappy rash can be the result of an allergic reaction to a product that has touched your baby’s bottom, such as a certain brand of nappy, perfumed baby wipes or a detergent used to wash a cloth nappy.
This is called allergic contact dermatitis. Sometimes it’s obvious what has caused the reaction, as the rash develops immediately after you’ve changed to a new product. On other occasions it may take you longer to work out the cause.
Occasionally, persistent nappy rash can also be caused by a food allergy or intolerance. If you suspect that a certain food may be contributing to your baby’s nappy rash, speak to your GP or health visitor.
How should I treat my baby’s nappy rash?
If your baby’s nappy rash is mild, and they don’t seem distressed, it’s fine to treat their symptoms yourself. Here’s how:
- Change your baby’s nappy often, every three hours to four hours, or as soon as possible after they’ve done a poo or a wee.
- Choose a super-absorbent nappy to reduce the amount of moisture next to your baby’s skin. Disposable nappies that are marked with a plus sign have added absorbency. If you use cloth nappies, add a booster pad, and avoid plastic nappy wraps. They can make the rash worse by locking in moisture.
- Make sure you’re using a nappy that fits your baby well. A tight nappy can trap more moisture against your baby’s skin, while a loose nappy can’t absorb moisture well enough.
- When you change your baby’s nappy, clean their genitals and bottom from front to back using water and cotton wool, or unscented, alcohol-free baby wipes.
- If your baby’s skin is broken or peeling, or very sore to the touch, try using a squeezy bottle of warm water to clean it gently without rubbing. Or squeeze a washcloth soaked in warm water onto their skin.
- Gently pat your baby’s skin with a soft towel until it's completely dry.
Apply a thin layer of barrier cream or ointment before putting on a clean nappy. You don’t need much. Just use a small amount and rub it in enough so you can still see your baby’s skin underneath. The cream will form a protective layer on your baby's skin, shielding it from wee and poo. If you’re not sure which one to buy, ask your pharmacist for advice.
- Give your baby as much nappy-free time as possible to let the air get to their skin. Lay them on a towel in a warm room, or leave their nappy off for a while at the end of a change. If they’re old enough to move around, put them down in a room with an easy-to-clean floor, or outside if it's safe and warm.
- A bath or top-and-tail wash once a day or twice a day at the most should be enough to clean your baby and look after their skin. Bathing them more often than this may dry out their skin and add to the irritation. Steer clear of soaps, bubble bath, lotions or talc as these may further irritate your baby's delicate skin.
If your baby is in childcare or being looked after by someone else, make sure they're aware that your little one has nappy rash and ask them to follow the same steps when changing your baby’s nappy.
If you think your baby's nappy rash could be a reaction to something you've used on their skin, try to identify it. If you've recently used a different washing powder, baby wipe or nappy, then change back to what you originally used to see if it makes a difference.
A mild case of nappy rash should clear up after about three days of home treatment following the above tips. It's important that you treat nappy rash, even if it isn't bothering your baby as it can become infected if left untreated.
How can I prevent my baby getting nappy rash again?
Nappy rash is common, so your baby may well have it again at some point. But the best defence against nappy rash is a dry bottom.
You can achieve this by following the same steps as you would for treating mild nappy rash. So, remember to change your baby's nappy regularly, clean and dry them thoroughly and apply barrier cream after each nappy change. And give them as much nappy-free time as you can to get some fresh air to the skin. And lastly, don't use talcum powder. It won't protect against nappy rash and can irritate your baby's skin.
Your baby can get nappy rash whether you opt for reusable or disposable nappies. However, some experts advise using a highly absorbent disposable nappy during an episode of nappy rash, to help keep as much moisture away from your baby’s skin as possible.
When do I need to call the doctor about nappy rash?
If your baby's nappy rash is spreading or getting worse, or if they’re in discomfort, see your GP, health visitor or practice nurse. Your baby may be prescribed a hydrocortisone cream to soothe the area. Ask your GP about whether you need to use a barrier cream as well as the hydrocortisone cream and when you need to apply it.
If your baby's nappy rash is caused by thrush, your GP, health visitor or practice nurse may advise you not to use barrier cream. Instead, they’ll prescribe a cream that's designed to clear up the fungal infection. If your baby has oral thrush, they may prescribe a gel or liquid medicine to treat it. Or if the nappy rash is caused by a bacterial infection, they may prescribe a course of antibiotics to help clear it up.

White spots or patches in your baby's mouth may be a sign of thrush. These patches will look a little like cottage cheese or milk curds. Your baby's mouth may be quite sore and they might be reluctant to feed.
Why has my baby got white patches inside her mouth?
It could be oral thrush, which is caused by the fungus candida albicans.
Oral thrush looks like white spots or patches of cottage cheese or milk curds in and around your baby’s mouth. These patches may appear:
- inside the cheeks
- on the roof of the mouth
- on the gums
- on the tongue
Thrush is most common in babies of 10 weeks and younger, but it can appear in older babies, too.
You can check that the white patches are thrush and not just milk residue. Gently rub a patch with a clean finger. Milk residue will wipe away easily. Thrush patches, on the other hand, may need to be rubbed a few times before they're removed. Once removed, you'll find a red, raw area underneath.
Your baby may not be bothered by thrush at all. But sometimes thrush can make your baby's mouth sore. You may first suspect thrush if your baby seems reluctant to feed, or keeps coming off your breast.
What has caused my baby’s thrush?
Thrush happens because the usual levels of candida fungus in your baby's mouth have increased and caused an infection.
Candida levels can increase because:
- Your baby's immune system is still immature, so she is less able to resist infection.
- She is having a course of antibiotics, which has reduced the levels of healthy bacteria in her body, allowing candida to spread.
- You're taking antibiotics, making you more prone to thrush. If you're breastfeeding, this makes it more likely that your baby will develop oral thrush.
Do I need to take my baby to the doctor for oral thrush?
It depends. If your baby's thrush is mild, and doesn't seem to be bothering her, you may not need to take her to the doctor. Sometimes, thrush just gets better on its own after a few days.
If the thrush doesn't get better, and seems to be putting your baby off feeding, see your doctor. Your doctor may prescribe an oral antifungal treatment, usually miconazole gel or nystatin suspension.
How can I treat my baby for thrush?
Apply the antifungal gel or the drops to the infected areas in your baby’s mouth after you've fed her. You'll probably need to do this up to four times a day. Put on a little of the treatment at a time, and try not to put the drops or gel towards the back of her throat, in case she gags.
Wash your hands each time you've finished treating your baby, to stop thrush from spreading.
Continue with the treatment for as long as your doctor advises, and for two days after the thrush has gone, to ensure it doesn't come back. Thrush should clear up after a week of treatment, but if it persists, see your doctor or health visitor for advice.
Your doctor will advise you to watch out for symptoms on your nipples. You may have thrush already, or there may be a chance your baby will pass it to you. If your nipples are sore, painful or itchy, put antifungal cream on after every feed, and wipe it off before you next feed your baby.
Treating yourself will protect you against breast pain. If your nipples are sore or cracked, thrush can spread into your breasts. This can be really painful, lasting for up to an hour after each feed.
If you have a severe case of nipple thrush, you may need to take antifungal tablets. You'll still be able to breastfeed, whatever treatment you're having.
If you express milk while you or your baby is being treated for thrush, give it to your baby before your course of treatment has finished. If you freeze the milk to use later, it may reinfect your baby with thrush.
Read more about breastfeeding and thrush.
Is there anything I can do to prevent my baby from getting thrush?
It's hard to prevent thrush. It's just one of those things that often happens to small babies.
However, some babies are more prone than others to the infection. Here are a few things you can try to keep thrush at bay:
- Clean and sterilise dummies, bottles and feeding equipment, and other toys she may put in her mouth, such as teething rings.
- Wash your hands after nappy changes, and have a separate towel for each family member.
- Wash your nursing bras at a high temperature and change your breast pads often. Thrush loves warm, moist, milky, environments
You could also try the following tips, but keep in mind that there's not much evidence that they work:
- Try giving your baby a drink of sterilised water after each feed. This rinses away milk left in her mouth, which the candida fungus thrives on. It's only worth trying after your baby is six weeks old and is used to breastfeeding.
- Put coconut oil, which has anti-fungal properties, on your breasts and nipples. Some mums swear by this, but it's not likely to get rid of thrush. You may want to check with your doctor or health visitor before trying home remedies for thrush.
Can thrush harm my baby?
Oral thrush in babies is not usually linked with other illnesses or conditions, and it usually clears up within a few days.
However, thrush can pass through your baby's digestive system to her bottom and cause nappy rash. The rash is often sore with red spots, and may take a while to heal.
You should talk to your doctor if your baby also has a fever of 38 degrees C or above if she is under three months, or 39 degrees C or above if she is between three and six months old. Your baby may have a different infection.
A bout of thrush can be trying for all of you. A hungry baby who finds it difficult to feed is always a worry, but thrush is usually short-lived.
Breastfeeding and thrush
What causes a thrush infection?
We all carry the fungus candida albicans in our bodies. It’s a normal part of our digestive system, and friendly bacteria usually keep it in check. But sometimes it gets a chance to grow and spread, leading to a thrush infection.
Breastfeeding creates the perfect environment for thrush. Thrush thrives in warm, moist, sugary places, which is exactly what your baby’s mouth is like during breastfeeding. The thrush infection can then pass to your nipples.
Thrush may take hold more easily if your nipples are sore or cracked because your baby isn’t latching on well. Unless thrush is treated, it can pass back and forth between you and your baby.
Thrush in the mouth is a common problem for babies, because their immune systems are still developing. It affects about one newborn in 20, and one baby in seven by four weeks of age.
Thrush is more likely to happen if you or your baby is having a course of antibiotics, as these suppress the healthy bacteria that keep the candida fungus in check. You're also more vulnerable to thrush on your nipples if you have vaginal thrush.
How will I know if I have thrush?
Common signs of thrush in breastfeeding mums are:
- Nipples that become more sore as you feed.
- A burning feeling in your nipples, especially when you've just fed your baby. The pain can last up to an hour after a feed.
- Itchy, ultra-sensitive nipples. Even loose, light clothing may feel uncomfortable.
- A change of colour in your nipples. They may become paler, or appear darker and shiny.
If the pain in your nipples can't be fixed by a better attachment with your baby, soothing with heat, or expressing, it's likely to be thrush.
You'll probably notice both your breasts are affected, unless you're in the very early stages of infection.
It's thought that thrush on your nipples can enter your milk ducts, the channels along which your milk flows to your nipple. It may cause shooting or burning pain deep in your breasts, that spreads down your arm or into your chest. This is called ductal thrush.
Other problems can cause sore, painful or cracked breasts, aside from thrush. It could be that your baby is not latching on well to your breast when he feeds.
Breastfeeding shouldn't be painful, so see your midwife, health visitor, lactation consultant or GP if feeding hurts or is uncomfortable.
How will I know if my baby has thrush?
If your baby has thrush, white patches that look like milk curds or cottage cheese will usually appear on his tongue, gums and on the inside or roof of his mouth.
These white patches do not wipe away easily, unlike a harmless coating of milk. If you touch the patches gently with a clean finger, you’ll find the base is raw and may bleed.
Your baby may be unsettled or only feed for a short time. He may pull away from your breast while feeding because his mouth is sore.
Thrush can pass through your baby’s digestive system to his bottom and cause nappy rash. The rash usually looks sore and moist with red or white spots, and may spread to the folds of the skin.
How is thrush from breastfeeding treated?
Your doctor will recommend that you and your baby are treated at the same time. She'll prescribe an antifungal cream or gel, usually Miconazole, for your nipples and your baby's mouth.
You need to spread a thin layer of cream over your nipples after every breastfeed. Wipe away any visible cream just before feeding your baby. It is safe for your baby, but it makes sense to wipe off any excess before he feeds.
Continue with the treatment for as long as your doctor advises, even if the thrush seems to have cleared up.
If your nipples are very sore your doctor may prescribe a mild steroid cream to help with healing.
To ease deep breast pain, you can take a mild painkiller, such as paracetamol, until the worst is over and your treatment starts to work.
Thrush pain and other symptoms should ease after two or three days. If they don’t, go back to your doctor. Persistent thrush and ductal thrush usually need treating for longer, sometimes for up to a month. Your doctor may prescribe antifungal tablets as well as cream for your nipples.
Severe thrush can lead to another infection by a common bacterium called staphylococcus. Like candida, staphylococcus lives on your body and usually doesn't cause problems. But if your nipples are damaged and already infected, it can spread. Your doctor may ask to take a swab of your breasts to check for a bacterial infection, and prescribe an antibiotic to treat it alongside your thrush treatment.
How can I stop thrush coming back?
- Sterilise dummies, bottles, teats, and breast pump parts, to avoid re-infecting yourself or your baby.
- Wash your hands often, especially after putting on the antifungal cream and changing your baby’s nappy.
- Use a separate towel for each person in the family, and wash them often at 60 degrees C. Or use paper towels for drying your hands and throw the towels straight in the bin.
- Wash anything that comes into contact with your breasts or your baby's mouth, such as bras, tops and bibs, at 60 degrees C, to kill the fungus. Sterilise, or wash in hot, soapy water, toys that your baby puts in his mouth. Replace toothbrushes that may be infected.
- If you're using breast pads, change them often.
You could try adding probiotics to your daily diet to help the friendly bacteria that suppress thrush to grow again in your digestive tract.
You can take probiotics in pill form, or by eating live, natural yoghurt, but don’t rely on them to fight your thrush infection. Antifungal treatment is the most effective way to get rid of it.
Some mums put live yoghurt on their nipples, but there's no evidence that this works to keep thrush at bay, or to treat it. If you try this home remedy, be sure to rinse off the yoghurt before feeding your baby, if he's less than six months old.
Can I still breastfeed?
It's fine to breastfeed your baby, and if you do so, you'll be doing really well, as it can be painful and difficult. It can be particularly upsetting if you've worked hard to get breastfeeding going, and now face worry and pain each time you feed.
If you're struggling, ask for help from your midwife, health visitor or GP. With treatment and support, you should soon recover and start to enjoy breastfeeding again.
You may find it easier to express for a couple of days, by which time your treatment should be working well. Expressing helps you to keep up your milk supply too.
You can feed your baby freshly expressed breastmilk during an outbreak, but don't freeze it, and throw away any milk you haven't used. Freezing breastmilk doesn’t kill off the thrush, and it’s sensible not to use milk that may have thrush in it while you are trying to clear the infection.

Papular urticaria is a mild allergic reaction to an insect bite or sting, often from fleas, mites or bed bugs. It causes itchy bumps around the site of a bite, which can sometimes develop into fluid-filled blisters. Papular urticaria usually looks red on white skin. On black or brown skin the colour difference may be less obvious, with the main sign being a raised area.
My baby was bitten or stung by an insect. Should I be concerned?
Insect bites and stings are usually nothing to worry about. In most cases, a cuddle and a bit of reassurance should help your baby forget all about it. Here's what to expect from the most common types of bites and stings:
Bees, wasps and hornets
A sting can be a nasty shock for your baby, but her discomfort shouldn't last. A little bump will appear on her skin, which may be sore or itchy at first. It will probably clear up within a few hours, though sometimes it can stick around for up to a week.
Mosquitoes, midges and fleas
Your baby may not notice straight away if she's bitten by a mosquito or similar insect. But a little while after the bite, a small red bump may appear, which can be quite itchy for your baby. The bump shouldn't cause any problems though, and will usually go away within a few days.
Horseflies
A horsefly bite can be very painful, so your little one will need plenty of cuddles and comfort. You'll probably notice a raised, red spot on her skin, and she may also develop other symptoms, such as hives, wheezing or swelling. If you have any concerns about her symptoms, or if the bite looks infected, see your GP.
Bedbugs
Bedbug bites aren't usually painful, though they can be itchy for your baby. They're most likely to appear on her face, neck, arms or hands, often as several little red bumps in a line. The bites usually clear up within a few days.
Spiders
Your baby is unlikely to be bitten by a spider in the UK, but it can happen. A spider bite will usually leave small puncture wounds on your baby's skin, and can become painful and swollen. If your baby develops other symptoms, such as vomiting and sweating, seek urgent medical advice straight away.
How do I treat an insect sting or bite?
A bite or sting can give your baby a shock, and may be itchy or painful, so she'll need plenty of cuddles and reassurance. If the insect is still around, swatting at it may prompt it to bite or sting again, so try to move away as slowly and calmly as possible.
If your baby's been stung by a bee, check to see if the sting is still in her skin. if so, scrape or flick it out with a credit card or the sharp edge of your nail. Don’t grasp it with your fingers or tweezers, as you may squeeze out more of the venom and make your baby's sting worse. Then simply follow the steps below.
For any type of bite or sting, follow these steps to reduce the risk of infection and help your baby feel better:
- Wash the area with soap and water, then press a cool, damp flannel over it for at least 10 minutes. This can help to reduce any pain or swelling and help your baby feel better.
- If a bite on your baby's arm or leg is causing any swelling, raising the affected area can help to reduce it.
- If possible, encourage your baby not to scratch her bite or sting. Keep her nails trimmed and clean to reduce any damage to her skin when she does scratch. You could also consider using anti-scratch mittens, or popping a pair of socks over her hands.
- If your baby is in pain from a big bite or sting, you can give her infant paracetamol or infant ibuprofen, provided she's old enough. Check the dosage information on the packet, or ask your pharmacist if you're unsure how much to give your baby.
In most cases, your baby's bite or sting should go down within a few hours or days. In the meantime, giving her plenty of cuddles and keeping her distracted with silly games and stories will help her forget all about it.
When should I take my baby to the doctor for an insect bite or sting?
Bites and stings usually clear up on their own, and don't need medical attention. However, sometimes they can cause an allergic reaction, or become infected.
See your GP if you have any concerns about your baby's bite or sting, particularly if:
- the bite or sting is near your baby's mouth, throat or eyes
- your baby's symptoms don't improve within a few days, or start getting worse
- there's a large, red, swollen area around the bite or sting
- the wound looks infected, for example if it's becoming increasingly red, swollen and painful, or starts leaking pus
- your baby seems generally under the weather, with flu-like symptoms such as a fever and swollen glands
Less commonly, an insect bite or sting can cause a serious allergic reaction, known as anaphylaxis. Call 999 for an ambulance if your baby has the following symptoms:
- swelling around her face, mouth or throat
- difficulty breathing
- fast heartbeat
- vomiting
- seems dizzy or faint
- becomes unconscious
I think my baby has a tick. How can I remove it?
A tick is a small, round insect with no wings. Although they usually live on animals, they can sometimes bite humans, too. They're most common in wild areas such as forests and woodland, but can also appear in parks and gardens.
Your baby probably won't notice if she's bitten by a tick, as the bites are usually painless. If she has been bitten, the tick will stay on her skin for up to a week. However, ticks can be hard to spot, as they're often as small as a poppy seed.
Tick bites are usually harmless, but they can sometimes spread a serious illness known as lyme disease. So it's a good idea to check your baby for ticks regularly, especially after spending time with her outside. You're most likely to spot one around her hairline and scalp.
If you notice a tick on your baby, try to remove it as soon as possible:
- Use a pair of fine-tipped tweezers to grab the tick as close to your baby’s skin as possible.
- Gently pull straight up until all parts of the tick are removed. Take care not to crush the tick's body, as this could make your baby's bite worse.
- After removing the tick, wash your hands with soap and water, and apply an antiseptic cream to the skin around the bite.
Don’t try to get the tick out by using petroleum jelly, alcohol, or a lit match, as these won’t work.
Ideally, once you've removed the tick, put it in a sealed container and send it to the government's tick recording scheme. This helps to keep track of lyme disease in the UK. If that's not possible, crush the tick using a hard object, being careful not to get any of its blood on your skin. Then just flush it down the loo, or wrap it in sticky tape and pop it in the bin.
If you’re worried about removing the tick yourself, take your baby to your GP or local walk-in centre. A doctor or nurse can remove the tick from your baby’s skin.
A tick bite is unlikely to cause any problems for your baby, but keep an eye on her as it heals. If she develops flu-like symptoms, or a red rash or ring forms around the tick bite and starts to spread, take her to the GP. It could be a sign of lyme disease, which can be serious if untreated, but will usually clear up with a course of antibiotics.
I'm taking my baby abroad. Should I be concerned about insects?
