It depends where you're going. In some countries, mosquitoes and other insects can carry serious diseases such as malaria. There are often vaccinations or other medicines available to protect you and your baby.
You can find out which countries pose a risk, and what vaccinations are available, on the NHS fit for travel website. The site also has lots of handy tips for minimising the risk of illness while you're away.
How can I prevent my baby from getting stung or bitten?
A few simple precautions can help to reduce the risk of your baby being bitten:
- Keep your baby's skin covered when she's outside, by dressing her in long sleeves and trousers, tights or leggings. Loose, flowing styles in natural fabrics such as cotton will be more comfortable for her in hot weather. This will also help to protect against sunburn.
- If your little one's started walking, make sure she wears shoes when she goes outside. Many bee stings happen when a person accidentally steps on a drowsy bee lying on the ground.
- If your baby's over two months old, apply insect repellent to areas of exposed skin, such as her face and hands. Ones containing 50 per cent DEET (diethyltoluamide) are the most effective. If you're in doubt, your pharmacist will be able to help you choose the best one for your baby.
- If your baby's under two months old, effective insect repellents aren't safe for her. Instead, it's best to keep her covered up with long sleeves and trousers, leggings or tights. You could also use a fine mesh net on her pushchair when you go out.
- Keep food and drinks covered when eating outdoors, particularly if they contain lots of sugar, as they can be a magnet for wasps and bees.
- Avoid using strong-smelling soaps, baby lotions or perfumes, as these can all attract insects.
- If you're taking your baby camping, pitch your tent well away from water such as ponds or lakes, which tend to attract mosquitoes.
- If your baby's been playing in a grassy or woody area, give her a quick check for ticks before bringing her inside.
- To protect your home from insects, keep windows and doors shut as much as possible. Or you could invest in thin netting to go over them, so you can still keep them open and get a bit of breeze.
- If your think your baby could have been bitten by bedbugs, check her cot with a bright torch. If there are bedbugs there, you may be able to spot them. Or you may notice tiny black specks, which could be bedbug droppings. If you do have a bedbug infestation, you'll usually need professional help to get rid of it. Your local council can help you find services in your area.
Take particular care in summer months (when insects tend to be most active), and near flowers, rubbish, compost, water and food, as these can all attract insects.
No matter how much care you take, the occasional insect bite or sting is just a normal part of life. Rest assured that it's very unlikely to do your baby any harm, and any shock or discomfort should soon pass.

In spite of the name, ringworm is caused by a fungal infection, and has nothing to do with worms. If your baby has it, they'll have a rash that looks like one or several rings, which can appear anywhere on the body. On white skin the rash will look red. On brown and black skin it will be a less obvious grey or brown. The rings will be crusty or scaly on the outside and smooth in the middle. They may also feel itchy. As the fungus grows, the rings get larger, ranging in size from about 1-5cm.
Ringworm can also affect your little one's scalp, though this is less common in young babies. Scalp ringworm can be dry and crusty, or moist and filled with pus. It is easy to confuse ringworm with dandruff or cradle cap.
Ringworm is a fungal skin infection that spreads easily among children. It causes a rash of ring-shaped inflamed patches on the skin, hence the name. It can be itchy and unpleasant, but it's easy to treat, often with an over-the-counter treatment. Personal and home hygiene can be key to preventing it, as the ringworm fungus lives on people, pets and surfaces.
What is ringworm?
Ringworm is an itchy fungal infection of the skin. It has nothing to do with worms. It's called ringworm because the infection appears as a rash in a ring or round shape.
Ringworm can be itchy, but it's not painful or dangerous. It's a fungal infection like athlete's foot and it's spread in the same way – by fungal spores. The fungus lives on people and animals, and in our environment. It spreads easily in built-up areas, and thrives in hot, humid weather.
Ringworm is more common in older children but newborns and babies can get it, and adults too.
Ringworm can infect the body or the scalp. But babies and children are more likely than adults to have a scalp infection.
What does a ringworm rash look like?
On your baby's body, look out for scaly, inflamed, slightly raised ring-shaped patches.
On brown or black skin, the infected areas may appear grey or darker than the surrounding skin. They appear more pink or red on white skin.
The rash tends to clear from the centre of the ring outwards, so you may find a raised scaly ring around more regular skin in the middle.
The ring sizes usually range between 1cm and 5cm, and can overlap. If ringworm isn't treated, the infection can spread, creating more, bigger ring-shaped patches to appear.
Ringworm on your baby's scalp may cause patches of their hair to fall out. Hairs growing out of the infected patch are brittle and break more easily. The patches may turn dry and crusty, or moist with little pus-filled sores.
How does ringworm spread?
Ringworm spores enter your baby's body through their skin. Your baby probably picked up ringworm from an infected person or pet, or from touching sheets, towels, toys, hairbrushes, or clothes that were carrying the fungal spores.
How should I treat my baby's ringworm?
Make sure it's ringworm before you treat it. Ringworm on the body can look like eczema, particularly a type called discoid eczema, which also forms rings.
See your pharmacist first. They should be able to confirm whether it's ringworm and advise on the best treatment. Ringworm is treated with an antifungal cream, gel or spray, depending on where it is on your baby's body.
Your pharmacist will explain how to use the treatment, and for how long. It's important to keep using the antifungal medicine for the correct length of time, even if your baby's rash has cleared up.
Your pharmacist can tell you whether you need to take your baby to the doctor for treatment. Your doctor may want to confirm the infection by taking a small sample of skin flakes from your baby's skin, or a hair sample to send to a lab. Your doctor may request samples from you and the rest of the family too, so you can all be treated together.
Creams, gels, or sprays don't always work well on scalp ringworm as these topical treatments can't get right into the hair roots. Instead, your doctor may prescribe antifungal tablets for your baby, and advise on a medicated shampoo that you can buy over the counter.
You can crush the tablets and mix them with a little water to give to your baby. The shampoo alone can't cure the infection, but it can help to stop it spreading and speed up your baby's recovery.
As well as treating your baby’s ringworm with medication, gently wash and dry the areas of ringworm on your baby's body every day. Be sure to wash between their toes and in their skin folds. Dry your baby's skin folds thoroughly, as the fungus thrives in moist, warm places.
Dress your baby in loose-fitting, cotton clothes that cover their legs and arms. Scratching can spread ringworm to other parts of the body, so keep your baby's fingernails short.
Can ringworm cause any complications?
It's highly unlikely that your baby will be affected by any complications, as long as their infection is treated.
Rarely, if severe scalp ringworm is not treated, it can lead to long-term hair loss. Ringworm on the body may lead to a bacterial infection, but usually only in people who have weakened immune systems.
How can I prevent a ringworm infection happening again?
The fungal spores can live for long periods. Make sure the whole family is checked and treated for ringworm. If you have a pet, check them for patches of missing fur, and take them to the vet for treatment.
To protect your baby and keep ringworm out of your home, follow these steps:
- Keep everyone's towels, sheets, clothes, hairbrushes, combs, hats, scarves, and toys separate.
- Disinfect items that are hard to keep separate and can't be washed, such as non-soft toys.
- Wash your baby's bedding, towels and hats at 60 degrees C.
- Make sure everyone in your home washes their hands regularly, and keep your baby's hands clean.
Should I keep my baby away from childcare?
Once you've started treating your baby's ringworm, you don't need to keep them away from their usual activities or childcare.

The first symptoms of roseola include:
- sudden fever
- runny nose, cough or sore throat
- puffy eyes
- swollen glands in your baby's neck
Your baby may also seem generally under the weather and not feel like eating much. Their fever may last for three days to five days before suddenly disappearing. Once the fever subsides a spotty rash will appears. On white skin the rash looks pinkish-red which may be less obvious on brown and black skin. It's most likely to start on your baby's chest, and tummy or back, before spreading to the face, neck and arms. It usually fades within a few days.
What is roseola?
Roseola is caused by a virus, usually human herpes virus type 6 (HHV-6). The tell-tale signs of roseola are a sudden, brief fever, followed by a rash, just when your baby seems to be getting better.
Roseola is common in babies aged between nine months and two years, but younger babies can get it too. It spreads via coughs and sneezes and from contaminated surfaces. Your baby can catch it from being near an infected person, from playing with toys, and from putting things in their mouth.
You probably won't be able to tell how your baby caught roseola, though. It's infectious before the rash shows. It can take nine days to 15 days for the rash to appear on your baby's body.
If your baby is in childcare, keep them at home until they're feeling better. There's no need to wait until the rash has disappeared, because they'll no longer be infectious at this stage.
What are the symptoms of roseola?
The first symptoms of roseola include:
- sudden fever of between 38 degrees C and 42 degrees C
- runny nose
- sore throat
- cough
- loss of appetite
- puffy eyes and swollen glands in the neck
- mild diarrhoea
Your baby's fever may last for three days or four days, before suddenly disappearing.
Once the fever goes, a spotty rash appears. It will start on your baby's chest, tummy and back, and may spread to their face, neck and arms. The rash is a pinkish-red on white skin. It may be harder to see on brown and black skin, and may appear as slightly darkened patches of skin. It will fade within a couple of days.
How can I treat my baby's roseola?
Roseola is a virus, so it probably just needs to run its course until your baby is better. Antibiotics won't help, because it's not a bacterial infection.
However, call your GP if:
- You're worried about your baby's symptoms. Because the fever appears before the rash, it's worth seeing your doctor to make sure your baby isn't ill for another reason.
- Your baby is under three months old and has a temperature of 38 degrees C or above.
- Your baby is between three and six months old and has a temperature of 39 degrees C or above.
- Your baby's rash hasn't got better after three days.
Otherwise, give your baby plenty of cuddles and comfort, and:
- Let them rest if they want to, but go with it if they'd rather be up and about.
- Give them lots of drinks to make sure they're well hydrated. Offer them regular breastfeeds. If they're formula-fed you can also offer extra cooled, boiled water.
- Keep them cool while they're napping, and at night. If the room they sleep in is warm, take a layer off them.
You can give your baby infant paracetamol or ibuprofen if the fever is making them uncomfortable, depending on their age:
They can have infant paracetamol from two months if they were born after 37 weeks and weigh over 4kg (9lb).
They can have infant ibuprofen if they're three months or older, and weigh at least 5kg (11lb).
Are there any complications of roseola?
The high temperature that comes with roseola can sometimes cause a febrile convulsion (fit).
It's scary to watch your baby having a convulsion, but it doesn’t usually cause any harm. If your baby hasn't had a fit before, take them to your nearest accident and emergency (A&E), just in case.
It's important to keep a close eye on your baby's symptoms. If you're worried that your baby has developed other symptoms and their condition is getting worse, see your doctor.
Can I catch roseola from my baby?
It's very unlikely. Most people have antibodies to roseola by the time they're four years old, whether or not they've had symptoms. This means you're unlikely to catch the virus from your baby.

The first sign of rubella is small spots that first appear on your baby's face and neck, and then spread elsewhere on their body. The rash looks red or pink on white skin. If your baby has brown or black skin, it can be harder to see the spots, like in the image above, but you may notice that your baby’s skin feels rough or bumpy.
Some children feel totally fine while they have rubella, but your little one may develop other symptoms, such as:
- aching fingers, wrists or knees
- fever
- a cough
- sneezing and a runny nose
- headache
- sore throat
- sore, red eyes
Rubella (German measles) in children ages one to five
What is rubella?
Rubella (German measles) is a contagious viral infection that causes a spotty rash. It isn't usually serious for children, and normally gets better on its own in about a week. However, it can be very dangerous for pregnant women, so you'll need to take some precautions while your child has it, such as keeping them away from school to minimise the risk of the infection spreading.
Thanks to the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, rubella is now uncommon in the UK. If your child has had both doses of the vaccine (offered at one year and again at three years and four months), they're unlikely to have rubella. However, children who have just had the one dose aren't completely protected yet, so some will remain at risk of catching it.
What are the symptoms of rubella?
The most obvious symptom is the rubella rash. It looks like lots of small pinkish-red spots on white skin. It can be harder to see on brown and black skin, but you may notice that your child's skin feels rough or bumpy. It usually starts out around the face and neck, before spreading to the rest of the body.
If your child has rubella, they may feel perfectly fine. Or they may feel generally under the weather, with swollen glands, painful joints, and flu-like symptoms such as fever, coughing and sneezing.
The rash usually goes away on its own, without treatment, in about three to five days. If your child feels generally under the weather, they should feel better once the rash has gone. If they have swollen glands, these can take a bit longer to go down, but should be back to normal within a few weeks.
How should I treat my child's rubella?
If you think your child could have rubella, take them to see your GP. Give the surgery a call first though, and let them know why you're booking the appointment. Rubella is very infectious, and can be dangerous for pregnant women. So your surgery may want to make sure that you don't end up sharing a waiting room with someone who's expecting, or hasn't had their vaccinations. They'll advise you on when and how you can safely go in for an appointment.
Rubella is caused by a virus, so antibiotics won't help. Instead, once your GP has confirmed that your little one has rubella, they'll give you tips on how to look after your child at home while their immune system fights off the virus.
Here's how to care for your child while they have rubella:
- Keep them away from school or nursery, and make sure they don't come into contact with any pregnant women, until at least five days after the rash first appeared. (If you or your partner is pregnant, see the section below: "How does rubella spread")
- Let them get plenty of rest if they want to.
- Encourage them to drink plenty of fluids, particularly if they have a fever.
- If their symptoms are causing them any pain, you can offer the correct dose of infant paracetamol or ibuprofen. Ask your pharmacist if you're unsure how much to give.
Your child should be back to their usual self within a week.
How does rubella spread?
Like many viruses, rubella is usually spread through coughs and sneezes. Your child will be most infectious until about five days after the rash first appears. During this time, you should keep them away from school or nursery.
Although the rubella virus is normally harmless, it can be very dangerous for pregnant women, leading to miscarriage or severe birth defects in the baby. If your child has rubella, they could still pass on the virus until about two weeks after the rash first develops, so try to keep them away from pregnant women during this time.
If you're pregnant, and have come into contact with someone who has rubella, call your GP surgery. They will offer you a blood test to check if you're immune to rubella. If not, you may be offered extra scans throughout your pregnancy, to check whether it's affected your baby. The good news is that you're extremely unlikely to catch it if you've had it before, or if you've had your MMR vaccinations. Learn more about rubella in pregnancy.
If your child has rubella, you can help prevent it spreading to any unvaccinated people in your family by:
- Encouraging them to use a tissue when they sneeze or cough, and binning the tissue straight away afterwards.
- Washing their hands often with soap and warm water.
How can I protect my child against rubella?
Make sure they receive both doses of the MMR vaccine. It’s usually given at one year - and again at three years and four months - as part of your child’s scheduled immunisations. If your child is behind on any of their immunisations, check with their doctor about a catch-up schedule.

If your baby gets scabies, they'll develop an extremely itchy, bumpy rash. The redness of the rash may be less obvious on brown and black skin but you should be able to feel it.
The rash often starts around the hands or feet, and can spread to the whole body. You may also notice little lines on your baby's skin.
What is scabies?
Scabies is a skin irritation caused by tiny parasitic mites that burrow under the skin. The bumpy rash you can see on your baby's skin is actually an allergy-like reaction to the eggs, saliva and poo the mites leave behind.
Scabies won't harm your baby, but it will make them itchy and uncomfortable.
Scabies doesn't go away by itself. The infestation will continue unless the mites are killed off. The mites' lifecycle is as follows:
- Female mites make burrows in the upper surface of the skin and use the burrows to lay their eggs.
- After about three or four days, the eggs hatch.
- The hatchlings move towards the skin's surface, where they mature into adults within 10 to 15 days.
- Once at the adult stage, the mites are ready for mating. A new generation of females creates new burrows to lay more eggs, and the lifecycle is repeated.
How does scabies spread?
The mites spread easily through skin-to-skin contact, such as by holding hands. Anyone can get scabies, and it makes no difference how careful you are about keeping clean. The mites don't wash off with soap and water, because they live just under the skin's surface.
Scabies often shows up in more than one family member or in groups of children in nursery.
What are the symptoms of scabies?
If your baby gets scabies, they will develop an extremely itchy rash. It will appear as scattered red bumps, usually between their fingers, around their wrists, on the outside of their elbows, and on their armpits, belly and genitals.
The rash may also show up on their scalp, face, kneecaps, the palms of their hands, and on the sides and soles of their feet.
You may see wavy, light-brown or silvery lines where the mites have burrowed under your baby's skin. They may also develop little pustules or pimples, or small, fluid-filled blisters.
The rash may look brown or black, and be harder to see, on black or brown skin. However, you should be able to feel it. You could also check paler areas of your baby's skin, such as their wrists, fingers, the palms of their hands and the soles of their feet.
If this is your baby's first bout of scabies, between two weeks and six weeks may pass between when the mites latch on to them and when they begin to itch.
If your little one has had scabies before, their reaction time will be much shorter, possibly within a few days. That's because their body is already sensitised to the mites' saliva and poo.
Should I take my baby to the doctor?
See your doctor if you think your baby has scabies. The sooner they're treated, the sooner they'll be more comfortable and no longer contagious.
The doctor will take a look at the rash. They may also do a painless test that involves scraping off a small sample of skin and looking at it under a microscope. Scabies mites, their eggs and their poo are visible when magnified.
Another test to detect the presence of mites is an ink test. Your doctor will rub a little ink on part of your baby's rash and then wipe it off with an alcohol pad. The ink seeps into the burrows and shows up as a line.
How should I treat my baby's scabies?
Your doctor will prescribe an insecticide cream that you'll need to spread over your baby's body. Even parts of their body that don't seem to be infected must be treated, so don't skip them.
The mites like to live in the folds of the skin. Be sure to put the cream between your baby's toes and fingers, under their nails, under their arms, in their navel and on their genitals.
You'll also need to apply the cream along your baby's hairline, and on their forehead, scalp and temples. Follow the directions for leaving the cream on their skin, usually for between eight hours and 12 hours, depending on the type of cream, and then wash it off.
It's best to put the cream on at bedtime and wash it off first thing in the morning. The mites are most active at night, so the treatment will be more effective if it's freshly applied in the evening.
It's important not to bath your baby just before applying the cream, as it works better when applied to cool, dry skin. If you put the cream on when your baby's warm and damp from their bath, it will soak too deeply into the skin's layers. You may need to adjust your baby's routine while you're treating them, if you usually give them a bath just before bedtime.
At other times, reapply the cream if it's washed off, for example, after you've cleaned your baby's bottom ready for a fresh nappy.
Keep your baby's fingernails short to prevent them from scratching their skin, so that the rash doesn't become infected. You could put mittens or socks on their hands at night if they're scratching. Mitts will also stop them sucking the cream off their hands.
It can take some time for the irritants in your baby's skin to go away after they've been treated. So they may be itchy for as long as three weeks after the mites have gone. If it's troubling your baby, see your doctor, who may prescribe an oral antihistamine or a cortisone cream for relief.
If your baby is still itching after four weeks, or if it gets worse and new burrows appear, see your doctor. They may advise you to repeat the treatment, or they may prescribe a different cream.
Are there any complications of scabies?
If your baby is scratching a lot, they may develop a bacterial infection, such as impetigo. Impetigo causes the rash to turn scabby. Your doctor can prescribe an antibiotic treatment.
Scabies can sometimes trigger eczema, or if your baby already has it, make it worse, because they're scratching a lot. You can use emollients to soothe your baby's eczema once the scabies treatment is over.
How can I prevent scabies?
The only way to prevent your baby from getting scabies is to avoid contact with anyone who may have it. This can be almost impossible, especially if your baby is around other children and has several carers. If your baby has been in close contact with another person you know has scabies, treat them straight away, even if they don't have the rash.
If your baby has had scabies, you'll need to prevent reinfection. Treat everyone in your house, as well as carers, even if they show no symptoms. It's best if everyone gets treated at the same time.
You'll also need to remove the mites from around your home as soon as you start treating your baby with the cream. Vacuum the floors and then dispose of the contents of the vacuum cleaner.
Wash your baby's clothing, towels, and bedding on a hot wash and dry them in a dryer, if you have one. Dry cleaning also kills the mites.
Seal any stuffed animals or toys that can't be washed in a plastic bag for at least three days. Scabies mites can't survive for more than a few days without a human host.
Can my baby go to nursery if he has scabies?
Your baby can return to nursery after one completed treatment with the cream. Tell them that your baby has scabies, so they can advise other parents that their children may need treatment.

If your baby has scarlet fever, their first symptoms will probably be:
fever
sore throat
swollen neck glands
Up to two days after your little one starts feeling under the weather, they'll develop the scarlet fever rash. This looks like small, raised bumps and starts on the chest and tummy, then spreads to the rest of the body. This makes your baby’s skin feel rough, like sandpaper.
The rash takes its name from its red appearance on white skin. While it may not appear red on brown and black skin, you'll still be able to see and feel the rough sandpaper texture.
Scarlet fever in children (ages one to five)
Scarlet fever is an infection caused by the bacteria streptococcus A. It causes a flu-like illness, a distinctive coating on the tongue and a rough sandpaper-like rash that spreads from the chest and tummy. Scarlet fever is contagious and most common in children. It is easily treated with antibiotics. Rarely, it can lead to a more serious illness, particularly if it is not treated.
What is scarlet fever?
Scarlet fever (scarlatina) is a contagious infection that usually causes a red rash, fever and sore throat. It's caused by a type of bacteria known as group A streptococcus (GAS), and is easily treated with antibiotics.
Your child is most likely to catch scarlet fever between the ages of two and eight, though babies, older kids and adults can also catch it. It's most common in winter and spring.
Although scarlet fever is less common than it used to be, it has been on the rise in recent years. Experts don’t know what's caused this increase in scarlet fever. However, a new strain of group A streptococcus started circulating in the UK in 2015, which soon became the most common cause of the disease. That strain may be the reason why rates of scarlet fever have continued to be high and why complicated cases have increased, too.
With more children being affected, it makes sense to learn the symptoms to look out for.
What are the symptoms of scarlet fever?
When your child first catches scarlet fever, they'll probably feel generally under the weather, with flu-like symptoms such as:
- a fever
- a sore throat (sometimes known as strep throat)
- swollen glands in their neck
- a headache
- unusual tiredness
- feeling or being sick
- a white coating on their tongue. As the infection progresses, this peels away, leaving the tongue looking red, swollen and bumpy
The characteristic scarlet fever rash usually appears about a day or two after your child starts feeling poorly. It looks a bit like sunburn, and has a rough texture that feels like sandpaper. The rash can be harder to see on brown or black skin, but you'll still be able to feel the rough texture.
The rash is most likely to appear first on your child's chest and stomach, before spreading to the rest of the body. It’s unlikely to spread to their face, but their cheeks may look flushed. As your child starts to get better, the skin where the rash has been may peel, like sunburn.
If you're not sure what's causing your child's rash, it's always a good idea to do the glass test. Press the side of a clear drinking glass to your child’s skin. A scarlet fever rash will fade to white under pressure. If the rash doesn't fade when you press a glass onto it, seek urgent medical advice, as it could be a sign of meningitis.
How is scarlet fever treated?
If you think your child could have scarlet fever, keep them home from nursery or preschool and see your GP. They may want to swab your child's throat, to check if it's scarlet fever, though this isn't always necessary.
Once your GP has confirmed that your child has scarlet fever, they will prescribe antibiotics to help them recover faster, and prevent the infection getting worse. Your little one should be back to their normal self within about a week after starting antibiotics. However, it's important to make sure they finish the whole course of treatment, which is usually about 10 days. Always follow your GP's instructions, as this will help to reduce the risk of any complications.
If your child is feeling well enough, they can go back to nursery or preschool 24 hours after they take their first dose of antibiotics. But they may still be under the weather, and need to stay at home for a few more days.
While your little one is recovering from scarlet fever, the following tips can help to keep them comfortable:
- Let them get as much rest as they want. Keep them away from nursery or preschool until at least 24 hours after their first dose of antibiotics.
- Encourage them to drink plenty of cool drinks, to soothe their throat and guard against dehydration. Water or your child's usual milk are the best options, but well-diluted fruit juice (1 part juice to 10 parts water) is fine, too.
- Offer your baby soft foods if they have a sore throat, but don't worry if they don't have much of an appetite while they're poorly. It's more important to make sure they get plenty to drink.
- If they're distressed or in pain, you can offer the recommended dose of infant paracetamol, or ibuprofen if that doesn't work. Your pharmacist can help if you're unsure how much to give and when. Don't give them medication to bring down a fever if they're otherwise feeling well, as the fever can help them fight the infection faster.
- If the rash seems to be itchy and uncomfortable for your little one, speak to your pharmacist. They may recommend calamine lotion or an emollient cream to soothe the itch.
In rare cases, scarlet fever can lead to serious complications such as pneumonia and meningitis, particularly if it's untreated. Although this is very unlikely to happen to your child, it's important to keep an eye on their symptoms, just in case. If you notice any new symptoms, or if they're not feeling better a week after starting antibiotics, take them back to see your GP.
How contagious is scarlet fever?
Scarlet fever is very contagious and can be easily passed on through coughs and sneezes, or by sharing common household objects.
Your child is unlikely to pass the infection on once they've been having antibiotics for at least 24 hours. Until then, keep them away from nursery or preschool and follow these tips to reduce the risk of scarlet fever spreading to the rest of your family:
- Encourage your child to cough or sneeze into a tissue where possible. Throw any used tissues in the bin straight away.
- Don't let them share cutlery, cups, towels, clothes, toys, bedding or bath water with anyone else.
- Wash their hands regularly with warm water and soap.
Can scarlet fever be dangerous for some people?
Scarlet fever mostly affects young children . Unfortunately, some people are at higher risk of developing complications from catching it, including:
- people who have a problem with the valves in their heart (valvular heart disease)
- people with a weakened immune system, such as those undergoing chemotherapy
- people with conditions that cause broken skin, such as chickenpox or impetigo
- people with pre-existing health conditions, such as diabetes
- women who have recently given birth
Where possible, try to keep your child away from these people until they've been taking antibiotics for at least 24 hours. If someone in your family is in an at-risk group, keep an eye out for symptoms of scarlet fever, and seek urgent medical advice if any appear. Getting treatment early reduces the risk of complications.
There's no evidence that getting scarlet fever during pregnancy can harm your baby. If you do develop scarlet fever while you're pregnant, your GP can treat you safely with antibiotics.
Other conditions caused by Group A Strep (GAS)
The same type of bacteria that causes scarlet fever can also cause other issues, usually respiratory (breathing) and skin conditions, including strep throat and impetigo . Very occasionally it can cause a serious illness needing urgent treatment called invasive group A strep, often known as iGAS. While this is rare, there have been more cases than normal in children since winter 2022 and the UK Health Security Agency have asked people to be alert to signs of worsening illness.
If your child has had scarlet fever, a sore throat, a respiratory infection, or generally seems unwell, contact NHS 111 or your GP if:
- they are getting worse
- they are drinking or eating much less than normal
- they have had a dry nappy for 12 hours or more or show other signs of dehydration
- they are under three months and have a temperature of 38°C, or are older than that and have a temperature of 39°C or higher
- they feel hotter than usual when you touch their back or chest, or feel sweaty
- they are very tired or irritable
Call go to A&E if:
- your child is having difficulty breathing, they may sound like they are grunting or you may see their tummy sucking under their ribs
- there are pauses when your child breathes
- their skin, tongue or lips are blue
- they are lethargic or floppy and will not wake up or stay awake

If your baby has slapped cheek syndrome, they may have a blotchy rash on one or both cheeks. A few days later, a rash may also appear on their chest, arms and legs. The rash can be raised and itchy. The redness that gives the rash its name may be less obvious on brown and black skin. Your baby may have a fever, runny nose and sore throat.
Slapped cheek syndrome is a mild childhood illness that can show up as a rash on your baby’s cheeks. Before the rash appears, your child is likely to feel unwell for a few days. Learn more about the symptoms of slapped cheek syndrome, how it can be treated, and if slapped cheek is dangerous in pregnancy.
What is slapped cheek syndrome?
Slapped cheek syndrome is a common childhood illness. It’s caused by a virus called parvovirus B19, and gets its name from the rash that appears on the cheeks of babies and children who catch it. The medical term for slapped cheek syndrome is erythema infectiosum.
Slapped cheek syndrome is also known as fifth disease, because it’s the fifth rash in a group of five rash diseases that also includes:
- scarlet fever
- measles
- rubella
- roseola
Like other viruses, such as colds and flu, parvovirus B19 spreads easily. Also, slapped cheek syndrome is only contagious before the rash appears, so it's hard to know who's got it and who hasn't.
How does slapped cheek start?
Your baby can catch slapped cheek syndrome from an infected person who coughs or sneezes near them. They can also pick it up if they touch something contaminated with the virus, and then put their fingers up their nose or in their mouth.
What are the symptoms of slapped cheek syndrome?
You'll probably first notice that your baby has a fever, a runny nose and is irritable and sleepy. They're also likely to have a sore throat, so may be grizzly about feeding.
Your baby is likely to feel unwell for a few days and may then develop a rash on one or both their cheeks. The rash looks red on white skin and may be less obvious on black and brown skin. A few days later, a spotty rash may appear on your baby’s body and limbs. The rash may make your baby feel itchy and uncomfortable.
However, some babies won’t have all of the symptoms of slapped cheek syndrome. Your baby may feel fine and just have the rash on one or both of their cheeks.
How long does slapped cheek last?
It takes about three weeks for slapped cheek syndrome to clear up. The rash on your baby's face usually fades within two weeks. The body rash also fades within two weeks, but can last for up to a month if your baby has been in the sun or becomes hot, perhaps after having a bath or being active.
Should I take my baby to the doctor if they have slapped cheek syndrome?
There's no need to take your baby to the doctor, because slapped cheek syndrome is a mild illness. It just needs to run its course until your baby’s better. Your health visitor or pharmacist can give you advice about treating your baby at home.
However, see your doctor if:
- You're not sure whether your baby's rash is caused by slapped cheek syndrome.
- Your baby’s fever reaches 38 degrees C or higher if they are under three months, or 39 degrees C or higher if they are under six months.
- Your baby's fever lasts longer than five days. They may have a different infection.
- Your baby is unwell in other ways, for example if they won't feed, or seems floppy.
- Your baby is dehydrated. They may have fewer wet nappies than usual, and no tears when they cry.
Slapped cheek syndrome can be more serious for babies with sickle cell disease or thalassaemia.
These disorders cause babies to have low levels of red blood cells (anaemia). Slapped cheek syndrome can make these types of anaemia suddenly worse. So call your doctor if your baby has one of these disorders and you think they have slapped cheek syndrome.
If you need to book a doctor’s appointment for your baby, tell the surgery about their slapped cheek syndrome before you go. Slapped cheek syndrome is very infectious, and can be dangerous for pregnant women. Your surgery may want to make sure that you don't share a waiting room with someone who's expecting or see a doctor who is pregnant. They'll advise you on when and how you can safely go in for an appointment.
How can I treat slapped cheek syndrome?
Slapped cheek syndrome is a virus, so it can't be treated with antibiotics. You can treat your baby at home as follows:
- Make sure they get plenty of rest.
- Encourage them to have their usual breastfeeds and formula feeds. If your baby is formula-fed or on solids they can have extra water, too. This will keep them hydrated.
- Infant paracetamol or infant ibuprofen can help bring down your baby’s fever. Your baby can have infant paracetamol from two months. If your baby was premature, or they're small for their age, check with your doctor or health visitor. They may recommend a lower dose. You can give your baby infant ibuprofen if they are three months or older, and weigh at least 5kg (11lb). Check the dosage information on the packet, or ask your doctor or pharmacist for guidance.
Once your baby has the rash, they're no longer contagious. If they're feeling better, it’s fine for them to return to nursery.
Can adults get slapped cheek syndrome?
If you’ve had slapped cheek syndrome before, it’s unlikely that you’ll catch it from your baby. Over half of adults are immune to slapped cheek syndrome and other infections caused by parvovirus B19.
If you do catch it, you may develop stiff and painful joints in your hands, wrists, knees and ankles. This joint pain can recur for a few weeks afterwards.
Adults don't usually get the distinctive facial rash, so you may just have flu-like symptoms and develop a rash on your body. Or you may not have any symptoms at all, so you won’t realise you have it.
Is slapped cheek dangerous in pregnancy?
To be on the safe side, see your doctor straight away if you're pregnant and you’ve been in contact with slapped cheek syndrome.
Most women who catch slapped cheek syndrome for the first time in pregnancy have healthy babies. But, rarely, it can cause serious complications. Your doctor can give you a blood test to find out if you have it now, or if you’ve had it in the past.
There’s a small risk of miscarriage if you have slapped cheek syndrome during the first 20 weeks of pregnancy.

Tonsillitis is an inflammation of the tonsils, the almond-shaped glands that bulge out on both sides of the back of your child's throat. You may be able to see it by looking into their mouth. Their tonsils may look swollen, and there may be white spots on them.
Other signs of tonsillitis include:
- a sore throat, which can make it hard for your little one to swallow.
- general cold and flu symptoms, such as a cough, headache, earache, or seeming generally under the weather
- fever
- swollen glands in their neck
- bad breath
Take your little one to your GP if you think they could have tonsillitis so they can double check what’s causing the symptoms. In most cases though, your GP will probably recommend that you take your child home and let them rest up until they feel better.
What is tonsillitis?
Tonsillitis is an inflammation of the tonsils – the two almond-shaped glands at the back of your child's throat.
If you encourage your little one to open wide and look in his mouth, you should be able to see his tonsils on either side of his throat. When they become inflamed, they can look red and swollen, and may develop white, pus-filled spots.
Tonsillitis is usually caused by a viral infection, but it can also be caused by bacteria. In most cases, it gets better on its own within a few days, without any treatment. It's very unlikely that your child will need to have his tonsils out, unless his tonsillitis keeps coming back.
What are the signs and symptoms of tonsillitis?
The main symptoms of tonsillitis in children are:
- a sore throat – you may notice that your child has difficulty swallowing, or starts losing his voice
- general cold and flu symptoms, such as coughing, headache, earache, nausea or feeling more tired than usual
- a fever of 38 degrees C or more
- swollen glands in your child's neck
- white spots on his tonsils
- bad breath
These symptoms usually pass on their own within three or four days, though in some cases they may need treatment with antibiotics.
How is tonsillitis treated?
If you think your little one could have tonsillitis, take him to the GP, so she can double-check what's causing his symptoms. She'll look at your child's throat and ask questions, to check if it's tonsillitis or something else.
Your GP may also offer to take a swab from your child's throat, to find out if his symptoms are being caused by a virus or bacteria. And if your little one's symptoms are particularly bad, she may also offer a blood test to check whether he could have glandular fever.
In most cases though, your GP will probably recommend that you take your little one home and let him rest up until he feels better. She may prescribe you some antibiotics, but tell you to only give them to your child if his symptoms don't improve within a few days. Or she may wait for the results of any tests before prescribing anything, since antibiotics only work on infections caused by bacteria, not viruses.
If your little one's symptoms don't get better within three or four days – with or without antibiotics – go back to your GP. She'll check to see whether there could be another reason for your little one's symptoms, and may prescribe a different antibiotic. Or she might refer you to an ear, nose and throat (ENT) specialist who can offer further tests and treatment if necessary.
Fortunately though, in most cases, your little one's tonsillitis will clear up on its own within a week.
How can I make my child more comfortable while he has tonsillitis?
The following tips may help your child feel better while he's under the weather:
- Let him get plenty of rest if he wants to. You'll probably also want to keep him home from school or nursery until he's feeling better.
- Offer him cool drinks – ideally water or milk - which will help to soothe his throat. Encourage him to drink plenty throughout the day to keep him well hydrated.
- If he's in pain, give him the correct dose of children’s paracetamol or ibuprofen. If you're unsure about the dose, check the pack or ask your pharmacist for advice.
Don’t give your child a salt water gargle. Although it can be helpful for adults, your little one is likely to swallow too much of the salty water, which isn't good for him.
Don't use over-the-counter throat sprays on your little one either, as these aren't suitable for children under six.
Is tonsillitis contagious?
The viruses and bacteria that can cause tonsillitis can be passed from person to person. To reduce the risk of your child passing tonsillitis to the rest of the family:
- Where possible, try to cover your child's mouth and nose with a tissue when he coughs and sneezes. If he's old enough, encourage him to do this himself, and to always keep a tissue handy.
- Always bin tissues straight after using them, to get rid of the germs.
- Wash your little one's hands frequently, especially after he coughs or sneezes.
If your child goes to nursery or preschool, you don't have to keep him at home, but he'll probably be too poorly to go in for a few days. You know your little one best, so use your own judgement as to whether he's feeling well enough to go in. It's also a good idea to give your childcare provider a ring, to let them know that your child has had tonsillitis.
Is tonsillitis ever serious?
It's very unlikely that tonsillitis will cause any problems for your little one. In most cases, it gets better on its own, or can be easily cleared up by a course of antibiotics.
However, in rare cases, tonsillitis can cause complications. And young children aged two to four are more at risk than older children, so it's wise to keep an eye on your little one's symptoms.
There are four main complications of tonsillitis to be aware of:
Other infections
Sometimes the infection that causes tonsillitis can spread to other parts of the body, leading to an ear infection, sinus infection or chest infection. If your little one develops new symptoms, or seems to be experiencing pain in areas other than his throat, go back to your GP.
Dehydration
If tonsillitis is making your child's throat sore, he may find it difficult or painful to swallow. Encourage him to keep drinking though, as young children can easily become dehydrated, particularly if they also have a fever.
Signs of dehydration in young children include:
- feeling very thirsty
- dark yellow, smelly wee
- not weeing very often
- dry mouth and eyes
- feeling unusually dizzy, lightheaded or tired
If think your little one could be becoming dehydrated, take him back to your GP.
Quinsy
Rarely, tonsillitis can progress to form a collection of pus (abscess) between the tonsils and the wall of the throat. The medical name for this is "peri-tonsillar abscess", but it's more commonly known as quinsy. Symptoms of quinsy include:
- a bad sore throat that gets worse quickly
- swelling inside your child's mouth and throat
- difficulty speaking, swallowing, opening his mouth or breathing
If you notice these symptoms, seek medical advice straight away. If you can't get hold of a GP, take your child straight to A&E. The doctor may drain the abscess with a small needle, or give your child antibiotics through a drip (intravenous antibiotics) to treat the quinsy.
Scarlet fever
Tonsillitis can be caused by lots of different viruses and bacteria. If your little one's tonsillitis was caused by streptococcus bacteria, he could also develop scarlet fever. However, this is very unlikely to happen to your little one.
Symptoms of scarlet fever include:
- A red rash on your child's chest and tummy, that feels rough to the touch. The rash is harder to see on darker skin, but you'll still be able to feel the rough texture.
- A white coating on the tongue, which leaves it red and swollen.
- Flushed cheeks.
If you notice these symptoms, call your GP surgery to let them know. Scarlet fever is very contagious, so your GP may just want to talk to you on the phone, rather than having you bring your child in. Learn more about scarlet fever.
If my child does have tonsillitis, will he need to get his tonsils removed?
It's very unlikely. An operation to remove the tonsils (tonsillectomy) used to be a common treatment for tonsillitis. But we now know that tonsillitis is likely to go away on its own, or with a short course of antibiotics, and most children grow out of recurrent tonsillitis eventually. So the surgery isn't usually necessary.
If your child keeps getting tonsillitis again and again (chronic tonsillitis), your GP will probably refer you to an ear, nose and throat (ENT) specialist. Your ENT specialist may recommend a tonsillectomy to prevent further episodes if your child gets tonsillitis:
- more than seven times in one year
- more than five times a year for two years
- more than three times a year for three years
What does a tonsillectomy involve?
Tonsillectomies are usually done on an inpatient basis. This means that your child will need to stay overnight in hospital.
The surgeon will remove your child's tonsils, and adenoids if necessary, through his mouth, so there won't be any scarring on his neck. Your little one will be asleep under a general anaesthetic during the operation, so he won’t feel anything. The procedure usually takes about half an hour.
Your child may be given fluids through a drip during and after the operation. He’ll then be taken to the recovery room, where the nurses will monitor him until he’s awake and doing well enough to head to the children’s ward to rest and recuperate. You'll probably be able to take him home the next day.
How should I care for my child once he’s home from surgery?
Your child’s throat will probably be quite sore for a week or two after the procedure. He may find it hard to swallow, have his teeth brushed, or eat certain foods. He may also complain of earache, as young children can find it hard to tell the difference between pain in the ear and pain in the throat.
To relieve these symptoms, it's a good idea to give your child infant paracetamol or ibuprofen every four hours to six hours, for the first 24 hours after his operation. This will help to keep him comfortable. Check the pack for how much to give, or ask your pharmacist if you're unsure.
After the first 24 hours, give your child painkillers when he needs them, provided you stick to the dosage described on the packet. You may find it particularly helpful to offer him a dose about half an hour before meals. This can soothe his sore throat and make it easier for him to eat and drink.
Let your child get plenty of rest, and encourage him to keep drinking throughout the day. Chilled drinks will be particularly soothing, but try to avoid acidic drinks, such as orange juice, as these can sting.
It may be tempting to give your child lots of soft foods after the operation, but it's best if he starts to eat normally as soon as possible. Eating his usual solid foods will help his throat to heal more quickly.
Keep your child away from school or nursery for about 10 days after the operation. This will reduce the risk of your child picking up an infection while his throat is healing.
Every operation carries a small risk of complications. Keep a close eye on your child after the procedure, and make an appointment with your GP if:
- he’s in a lot of pain, and the recommended dose of children's painkillers doesn't seem to help
- he has a fever of 38 degrees C or more that doesn't come down with paracetamol or ibuprofen
- he's refusing to drink
- the area starts to bleed
- he brings up brown, red, or black vomit
For most children, however, a tonsillectomy won't be necessary. Your child's tonsillitis should soon pass – just be ready with plenty of sympathy and cool drinks in the meantime.
When your child has a sore throat, it can be difficult to tell the difference between mild tonsillitis and the common cold or flu.

If your baby has common warts, they're most likely to appear on their hands, though they can appear elsewhere. They look like raised, grainy bumps. The bumps will probably be the same colour as your baby's skin, but they may also be lighter or darker. The warts often contain one or more little black dots.
There are other types of warts, too:
- Flat warts are smaller and smoother than common warts. They are most likely to appear on your baby's face.
- Verrucas (plantar warts). These are likely to appear on the soles of your baby's feet and can be quite painful.
Most warts will go away without treatment within a couple of months, although some can take several years. Warts can sometimes be treated if they bother your baby so talk to your pharmacist if you're worried.
Verrucas are small warts, often with a black speck in the centre, that are found on the soles of the feet. They're most often picked up at swimming pools. If your toddler gets a verruca, it's fine to leave it to clear up by itself. They usually disappear within two years.
If the verruca is painful for your toddler though, you can treat it with salicylic acid. You can buy this over the counter or get it on prescription from the practice nurse at your GP surgery.
